                              ## 🧠 **The Logic of Intervention Selection: From Test Finding to Treatment**

                              The **goal of vestibular rehabilitation** is **not** to “do exercises” — it is to **promote neuroplasticity**, **restore gaze stability**, **improve balance**, and **reduce dizziness** through **targeted, mechanism-specific interventions**.

                              Every intervention in **Group II (Clinical Treatments)** is designed to address a **specific neurologic impairment** identified in **Group I (Tests)**.

                              You do **not** prescribe **CT1–CT7** randomly.  
                              You prescribe them **because a test showed a deficit**.

                              ---

                              # 🔁 **Step 1: General Framework — How Test Findings Drive Treatment**

                              | **Test Domain** | **Key Tests** | **What It Assesses** | **If Abnormal, Consider These Interventions** |
                              |----------------|--------------|------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
                              | **Ia. Oculomotor** | Smooth Pursuit, Saccades, Convergence, Cover Test | Integrity of brainstem, cerebellum, and visual-vestibular integration | CT2, CT3, CT5, CT6, CT7 |
                              | **Ib. VOR Testing** | HIT, DVA, VOR Cancellation | Vestibular-ocular reflex function | CT1, CT2, CT4, CT5 |
                              | **Positional Testing** | Dix-Hallpike, Roll Test | Presence of BPPV | **Not in Group II** — use canalith repositioning (Group IV or VI) |

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Directive**:  
                              > *"Oculomotor exercises should be used in the event that we identify abnormal findings in the oculomotor component of our exam."*  
                              > This means: **No abnormal finding = no isolated oculomotor exercise**.

                              ---

                              # 🔁 **Step 2: Specific Test Findings and Their Corresponding Interventions**

                              We will now go **one by one** through the **positive findings** in **Ia and Ib**, and link them to **II.CT1–CT7**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 1: Abnormal Smooth Pursuit (Ia.V3)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - The patient cannot smoothly track a moving target.
                              - The eyes move in a **saccadic (jumpy)** pattern.
                              - This suggests **cerebellar dysfunction** or **brainstem pathology**.

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Connection**:  
                              > *"Smooth pursuit: examine the ability to smoothly track a target."*  
                              > Abnormal pursuit is a **central red flag**.

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **CT2. VOR Cancellation (Visual Motion Sensitivity)**  
                                - Why: Forces the patient to maintain gaze on a stationary target while the head moves — challenges the **cancellation mechanism** in the brainstem.
                                - Dose: 3 sets of 1 min, 2x/day
                              - **CT5. Eye Head Saccade Exercises**  
                                - Why: Improves coordination between eye and head movements — trains **saccadic accuracy** and **predictive control**.
                                - Example: “Look at the red spot, then quickly turn your head and look at the blue spot.”
                              - **CT6. Imaginary Targets (Remembered Targets)**  
                                - Why: Engages **cognitive-vestibular integration** — useful if pursuit is poor due to attention or memory issues.

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**:
                              - **Isolated smooth pursuit exercises without head movement**  
                                - Why: NM.txt states: *"Clinicians should not offer saccadic or smooth-pursuit eye exercises in isolation (i.e., without head movement) as specific exercises for gaze stability..."*  
                                - Isolated eye movements **do not drive VOR adaptation** and lead to **poorer outcomes**.

                              > 💡 **Clinical Pearl**:  
                              > If smooth pursuit is abnormal, **do not assume BPPV** — consider **central pathology** first.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 2: Abnormal Saccades (Ia.V4)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - Saccades are **dysmetric** (overshoot or undershoot) or **slow**.
                              - Suggests **frontal lobe, cerebellar, or brainstem dysfunction**.

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **CT5. Eye Head Saccade Exercises**  
                                - Why: Trains **predictive saccades** with head movement — improves **spatial accuracy**.
                                - Example: “When I say ‘go,’ look at the target and turn your head at the same time.”
                              - **CT6. Imaginary Targets**  
                                - Why: Forces the brain to **recall spatial location** without visual input — enhances **internal mapping**.
                              - **CT7. Brock String**  
                                - Why: Provides **visual feedback** for saccadic accuracy — helps patient see when they’re missing the target.

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**:
                              - **Isolated horizontal saccades without head movement**  
                                - Why: Again, **no head movement = no VOR engagement** → ineffective for gaze stability.

                              > 📌 **UpRuperta.txt Connection**:  
                              > *"VOMS > 2 on Saccades" = Impaired oculomotor function* → justifies use of **CT5, CT6, CT7**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 3: Impaired Convergence (Ia.V5)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - Patient cannot cross eyes for near vision.
                              - Near Point Convergence (NPC) > 6 cm.
                              - Common in **concussion, brain injury, or cervical dysfunction**.

                              > 📌 **NM.txt & UpRuperta.txt**:  
                              > *"Near Point Convergence > 6 cm" = Impaired oculomotor function*

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **CT3. VOR Plus Vergence**  
                                - Why: Combines **head movement** with **convergence** — trains the brain to **integrate vestibular and vergence systems**.
                                - Example: “Move the pen toward your nose while doing VORx1.”
                              - **CT7. Brock String**  
                                - Why: Provides **binocular feedback** — patient sees if they are seeing one or two strings.
                                - Helps improve **vergence timing and accuracy**.

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**:
                              - **Convergence exercises alone (pencil push-ups)**  
                                - Why: Isolated convergence training **does not address vestibular integration**.
                                - Must be **paired with head movement** to be effective.

                              > 💡 **Clinical Pearl**:  
                              > Poor convergence + dizziness with reading = **visual-vestibular mismatch** → treat with **CT3 and CT7**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 4: Positive Head Impulse Test (HIT) (Ib.V8)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - **Catch-up saccade** after head thrust → **unilateral vestibular hypofunction (UVH)**
                              - The **VOR is impaired** on the side **toward which the head is thrown**

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"HIT is + to left" = Left vestibular hypofunction*

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **CT1. VOR x1 (Gaze Stability)**  
                                - Why: The **gold standard** for VOR adaptation.
                                - Dose: 20–35 min/day over 4–5 sessions (NM.txt)
                              - **CT4. Head Impulse Exercise**  
                                - Why: Small, controlled head impulses → promotes **high-frequency VOR adaptation**.
                                - Progress from **seated → standing → walking**.
                              - **CT5. Eye Head Saccade Exercises**  
                                - Why: Improves **spatial awareness** during rapid head turns.

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**:
                              - **Isolated saccades or pursuits without head movement**  
                                - Why: **Ineffective** for UVH — must **challenge the VOR**.

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Evidence**:  
                              > *"Strong evidence supports GSE for individuals with UVH."*

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 5: Dynamic Visual Acuity (DVA) Loss ≥ 3 Lines (Ib.V11)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - Patient loses visual acuity when head moves → **impaired VOR**
                              - Can be due to **unilateral or bilateral vestibular hypofunction**

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"DVA loss of 4 lines" = Indication for VOR adaptation*

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **CT1. VOR x1**  
                                - Why: Directly trains gaze stability during head movement.
                              - **CT4. Head Impulse Exercise**  
                                - Why: High-acceleration movements → improves **reflexive VOR response**.
                              - **CT2. VOR Cancellation**  
                                - Why: If patient also has **visual motion sensitivity**, this helps **reduce over-reliance on vision**.

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**:
                              - **Static balance exercises alone**  
                                - Why: DVA is a **gaze stability** issue — must **move the head** to improve it.

                              > 💡 **Clinical Pearl**:  
                              > DVA loss + gait imbalance = **high fall risk** → combine **CT1 + FGA progression**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 6: Positive VOR Cancellation (Ib.V2)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - Patient reports **dizziness or visual motion sensitivity** when moving head while fixating on a stationary target.
                              - Indicates **impaired ability to suppress the VOR** — common in **central disorders** or **chronic vestibular loss**.

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Increase symptoms with VOR Cancellation" = Visually-induced dizziness*

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **CT2. VOR Cancellation (Visual Motion Sensitivity)**  
                                - Why: **Habituation and adaptation** to conflicting visual-vestibular input.
                                - Start **seated**, progress to **standing**, then **walking**.
                                - Use **complex backgrounds** (e.g., grocery store, busy street).
                              - **CT6. Imaginary Targets**  
                                - Why: Reduces reliance on visual input — trains **internal spatial mapping**.
                              - **CT7. Brock String**  
                                - Why: Helps patient **disambiguate visual motion** — useful if they confuse **self-motion** vs. **object motion**.

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**:
                              - **Avoid visual motion exposure**  
                                - Why: This **worsens** visual motion sensitivity — must **gradually expose**.

                              > 📌 **UpRuperta.txt**: *"Visually-induced dizziness" = Indication for CT2*

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Finding 7: Spontaneous Nystagmus (Ia.V2)**

                              #### 🧠 **What It Means**:
                              - Nystagmus present at rest, without head movement.
                              - Suggests **central pathology** (e.g., brainstem stroke, MS) or **acute peripheral loss**.

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Spontaneous nystagmus in room light which beats to the RIGHT"*

                              #### ✅ **Appropriate Interventions**:
                              - **Only if peripheral**: CT1, CT4 (VOR adaptation)
                              - **If central**: **Refer immediately** — do **not** treat with CT1–CT7 without medical clearance

                              > 💡 **Clinical Pearl**:  
                              > Spontaneous nystagmus + **gaze-evoked** = **central**  
                              > Spontaneous nystagmus + **HIT+** = **peripheral** (acute UVH)

                              ---

                              # 🔁 **Summary: From Test Finding to Treatment Prescription**

                              | **Test Finding** | **Indicates** | **Use Intervention** | **Why** | **Evidence Source** |
                              |------------------|--------------|----------------------|--------|--------------------|
                              | Abnormal Smooth Pursuit | Cerebellar/brainstem dysfunction | CT2, CT5, CT6 | Improves smooth tracking with head movement | NM.txt: No isolated eye exercises |
                              | Abnormal Saccades | Frontal/cerebellar dysfunction | CT5, CT6, CT7 | Improves accuracy and spatial mapping | UpRuperta.txt: VOMS >2 on saccades |
                              | Impaired Convergence (NPC >6 cm) | Vergence dysfunction | CT3, CT7 | Integrates VOR and vergence systems | UpRuperta.txt: NPC >6 cm |
                              | Positive HIT | Unilateral vestibular hypofunction | CT1, CT4, CT5 | Promotes VOR adaptation | NM.txt: GSE for 20–35 min/day |
                              | DVA Loss ≥3 Lines | VOR impairment | CT1, CT4 | Improves gaze stability | NM.txt: DVA loss of 4 lines |
                              | Positive VOR Cancellation | Visual motion sensitivity | CT2, CT6, CT7 | Reduces visual dependence | NM.txt: Increase symptoms with VOR Cancellation |
                              | Spontaneous Nystagmus | Central or acute peripheral loss | CT1–CT7 only if peripheral | Do not treat central without referral | NM.txt: Spontaneous nystagmus |

                              ---

                              # 🔁 **Final Clinical Algorithm: How to Choose Interventions in Practice**

                              1. **Start with Oculomotor Screen (Ia)**  
                                 - If **abnormal**, add **CT2, CT3, CT5, CT6, CT7** as indicated
                              2. **Test VOR (Ib)**  
                                 - If **HIT+ or DVA loss**, add **CT1, CT4**
                                 - If **VOR Cancellation+**, add **CT2**
                              3. **Do NOT use isolated eye exercises** — always **pair with head movement**
                              4. **Dose GSE (CT1, CT4) at 20–35 min/day over 4–5 sessions** (NM.txt)
                              5. **Progress from static → dynamic → functional**
                              6. **Reassess every 1–2 weeks** with FGA, DVA, VOMS

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Practice Summary**:  
                              > *"Clinicians should not offer saccadic or smooth-pursuit eye exercises in isolation... without head movement."*

                              # 🧠 **The Logic of Posterior Canal BPPV Testing and Treatment: A Hierarchical Decision-Making Framework**

                              The goal is **not** to perform every test or every maneuver — it is to **diagnose with precision** and **treat with efficiency**, using the **least invasive, most effective method**.

                              We follow a **stepwise, evidence-based algorithm**:

                              > **Test → Confirm → Treat → Re-test → Rehabilitate**

                              Each step is **guided by the previous one**.

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Part 1: Choosing Among Posterior Canal BPPV Positional Tests (III.BPPV.1–4)**

                              You do **not** perform all four tests. You choose **one primary test** based on:
                              - **Patient safety**
                              - **Cervical spine status**
                              - **Symptom severity**
                              - **Clinical setting**
                              - **Need for diagnostic clarity**

                              Let’s examine each test and its **indications, advantages, and limitations**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **III.BPPV.1. Dix-Hallpike Test – The Gold Standard**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Dix-Hallpike is the gold standard for the diagnosis of posterior canal BPPV."*  
                              > *"Clinicians should diagnose posterior canal BPPV when vertigo associated with torsional upbeating nystagmus is provoked by the Dix-Hallpike maneuver."*

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It:**
                              - **First-line test** for suspected posterior canal BPPV
                              - Patient has **no cervical spine pathology**
                              - No severe orthostatic hypotension
                              - Can tolerate rapid supine transition

                              #### 🔹 **Procedure Recap:**
                              1. Patient sits, head turned 45° toward side being tested
                              2. Rapidly lowered to supine with head extended ~30° below table edge
                              3. Observe for **nystagmus and vertigo** over 30–60 sec
                              4. Return to sitting with **PT holding patient for 30–60 sec after**

                              #### 🔹 **Positive Finding:**
                              - **Torsional-upbeating nystagmus** (rotational component toward lower ear, vertical component upward)
                              - **Latency**: 2–10 seconds
                              - **Fatigability**: Diminishes with repetition
                              - **Direction-changing on return to sitting** (in cupulolithiasis)

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"A positive test indicates right posterior canal BPPV when right Dix-Hallpike provokes right torsional-upbeating nystagmus."*

                              #### ❌ **When NOT to Use:**
                              - Cervical instability, recent neck surgery, severe arthritis
                              - Uncontrolled hypertension, recent stroke
                              - Severe orthostatic hypotension

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **III.BPPV.3. Modified Dix-Hallpike Test With Head Over Pillow**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Place the person in the middle of the bed. Turn their head 45 degrees and lie them over the pillow. The sensitivity of the test was 96% and the specificity was 88%."*

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It:**
                              - Patient has **cervical spine limitations** but still needs posterior canal assessment
                              - Standard Dix-Hallpike is **too provocative** (e.g., severe vertigo, nausea)
                              - You want **greater head extension** to enhance nystagmus

                              #### 🔹 **Why It Works:**
                              - The **pillow allows greater head extension** than the table edge
                              - This **increases gravitational pull** on otoconia in the posterior canal
                              - May **prolong nystagmus duration** and **intensify symptoms**, making diagnosis easier

                              > 💡 **NM.txt Insight**: *"It may result in longer duration of nystagmus and more intense symptoms, hopefully making the diagnosis easier for you to see."*

                              #### 🔹 **Positive Finding:**
                              Same as standard Dix-Hallpike:
                              - **Torsional-upbeating nystagmus** toward the lower ear
                              - Latency, fatigability, direction change

                              #### ❌ **When NOT to Use:**
                              - Patient cannot lie flat
                              - Severe cervical pain with extension

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **III.BPPV.4. Sidelying Test**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Sidelying Test" is listed as an alternative.*

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It:**
                              - **Contraindication to supine positioning** (e.g., severe cervical spine disease, obesity, respiratory compromise)
                              - Patient **cannot tolerate head extension**
                              - Used in **bedbound or acutely ill patients**

                              #### 🔹 **Procedure:**
                              1. Patient starts sitting, head turned 45° toward side being tested
                              2. **Roll directly to side-lying** (affected ear down), **without going supine**
                              3. Observe for nystagmus and vertigo
                              4. Return to sitting

                              #### 🔹 **Positive Finding:**
                              - Same **torsional-upbeating nystagmus** as Dix-Hallpike
                              - May be **less intense** due to reduced canal alignment

                              #### 🔹 **Why Use It?**
                              - **Safer** than Dix-Hallpike in high-risk patients
                              - Still aligns posterior canal with gravity vector
                              - Useful when **standard test is contraindicated**

                              > 💡 **Clinical Pearl**:  
                              > If Sidelying Test is positive, you can **still treat with Epley or Semont** — the **mechanism is the same**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **III.BPPV.2. Loaded Dix-Hallpike**

                              > Not explicitly detailed in NM.txt, but implied as a **more provocative variant**.

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It:**
                              - **Suspected cupulolithiasis** (non-fatiguing nystagmus)
                              - **Weak or equivocal response** on standard Dix-Hallpike
                              - Need to **increase gravitational force** on otoconia

                              #### 🔹 **How It’s Done:**
                              - Same as Dix-Hallpike, but with **added head weight** (e.g., sandbag, hand pressure)
                              - Increases **inertial force** on debris

                              #### ❌ **Risks:**
                              - Increased vertigo and nausea
                              - Cervical strain
                              - Not recommended in elderly or frail patients

                              > 💡 **Use Sparingly**: Only when **diagnosis is uncertain** and **other tests are negative**.

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Summary: Choosing the Right Test for the Right Patient**

                              | Patient Presentation | Recommended Test | Why |
                              |----------------------|------------------|-----|
                              | Healthy, no neck issues | **Dix-Hallpike** | Gold standard, high sensitivity |
                              | Neck pain, limited extension | **Modified Dix-Hallpike (with pillow)** | Allows greater extension, safer |
                              | Cervical instability | **Sidelying Test** | Avoids supine extension |
                              | Weak nystagmus on standard test | **Loaded Dix-Hallpike** | Increases gravitational force |
                              | Bedbound, acutely ill | **Sidelying Test** | Feasible in limited mobility |

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Connection**:  
                              > *"A negative Dix-Hallpike does not necessarily rule out posterior canal BPPV."*  
                              > → So if negative but suspicion remains, **repeat with Modified or Sidelying Test**.

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Part 2: From Positive Test to Treatment – Choosing the Right CRM (IV.PCCRM.1–4)**

                              Now that you’ve confirmed **posterior canal BPPV**, you must choose a **canalith repositioning maneuver (CRM)**.

                              From **NM.txt**:  
                              > *"Canalith repositioning procedures are strongly recommended for treatment of posterior canal BPPV."*  
                              > *"Modified Epley, Semont Plus, and Li Maneuver are supported by strong evidence."*

                              Let’s examine each:

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **IV.PCCRM.1. Modified Epley Maneuver – First-Line Choice**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Modified Epley (first choice)"*  
                              > *"Strong recommendation by clinical practice guideline"*

                              #### ✅ **When to Use:**
                              - **First-line treatment** for posterior canal BPPV
                              - Patient can tolerate **four-position sequence**
                              - No cervical spine or cardiovascular contraindications

                              #### 🔹 **Mechanism:**
                              - Rotates the posterior canal **into alignment with the common crus**
                              - Uses gravity to move otoconia **from canal → utricle**

                              #### 🔹 **Steps:**
                              1. **Dix-Hallpike position** (affected ear down)
                              2. **Head turned 90° to midline**
                              3. **Body turned 90° to unaffected side**
                              4. **Sit up**

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Directive**:  
                              > *"The PT then HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT as they come to sitting, and continues holding onto them for up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver."*

                              #### ❌ **When NOT to Use:**
                              - Severe cervical arthritis
                              - Obesity (hard to roll)
                              - Severe vertigo/nausea (may not tolerate full sequence)

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **IV.PCCRM.2. Semont Maneuver – Fast, High-Velocity Alternative**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Semont Plus" is listed as an evidence-based option*

                              #### ✅ **When to Use:**
                              - Patient **cannot tolerate slow Epley**
                              - Need **rapid treatment** (e.g., in acute care)
                              - Epley failed or was poorly tolerated

                              #### 🔹 **Mechanism:**
                              - **Rapid lateral throw** from affected side to unaffected side
                              - Uses **inertial force** to "sling" otoconia out of the canal

                              #### 🔹 **Steps:**
                              1. Sit, head turned 45° **away** from affected side
                              2. Rapidly lie down on **affected side** (head extended)
                              3. **Quickly throw** to opposite side, face down
                              4. Sit up

                              #### 🔹 **Advantages:**
                              - Faster than Epley
                              - Fewer positions
                              - Effective in **obese or immobile patients**

                              #### ❌ **Risks:**
                              - High velocity → risk of **cervical injury**
                              - May provoke **severe vertigo/nausea**
                              - Not for frail or elderly patients

                              > 📌 **NM.txt Warning**: *"Caution should be taken... in those with comorbidities."*

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **IV.PCCRM.3. Semont Plus**

                              > A **modified Semont** with **longer hold times** or **additional steps**.

                              #### ✅ **When to Use:**
                              - Standard Semont **failed**
                              - Suspected **cupulolithiasis** or **multicanal BPPV**
                              - Need **more force** to dislodge debris

                              #### 🔹 **Why "Plus"?**
                              - Longer duration in each position
                              - May include **additional head movements**
                              - Increases chance of success in **intractable cases**

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Semont Plus" is listed as an evidence-based option*

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **IV.PCCRM.4. Li Maneuver – For Cervical Spine Limitations**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Li Maneuver" is listed as an evidence-based option*

                              #### ✅ **When to Use:**
                              - **Cervical spine disease** (e.g., stenosis, fusion, arthritis)
                              - Patient **cannot extend neck**
                              - Epley and Semont are **contraindicated**

                              #### 🔹 **Mechanism:**
                              - Patient **stays upright**
                              - Head is rotated and **tilted** to use gravity in a **non-supine position**
                              - Otoconia move from posterior canal → utricle without full supine transition

                              #### 🔹 **Steps:**
                              1. Sit, head turned 45° to affected side
                              2. **Tilt head 60° downward** (chin to chest)
                              3. **Rotate head 110° to opposite side**
                              4. **Lift head to neutral**, then sit up

                              #### 🔹 **Advantages:**
                              - **No supine position** → safe for cervical spine
                              - Low risk of vertigo
                              - Can be **self-administered**

                              #### ❌ **Limitations:**
                              - Less studied than Epley
                              - May be **less effective** in severe cases

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Li Maneuver" is listed as an evidence-based option*

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Summary: Choosing the Right CRM Based on Test and Patient Factors**

                              | Test Result | Patient Factors | Recommended CRM | Why |
                              |------------|----------------|------------------|-----|
                              | Positive Dix-Hallpike | Healthy, no neck issues | **Modified Epley** | First-line, high success rate |
                              | Positive Dix-Hallpike | Frail, elderly, nauseated | **Li Maneuver** | Safer, no supine, no extension |
                              | Positive Dix-Hallpike | Obese, immobile | **Semont Plus** | Fewer positions, faster |
                              | Positive Sidelying Test | Cervical instability | **Li Maneuver** | Avoids neck extension |
                              | Failed Epley | Persistent symptoms | **Semont Plus or Li** | Alternative biomechanics |
                              | Bilateral BPPV | Positive on both sides | **Epley on each side** | Treat sequentially, re-test |

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"If the patient does not respond within 4 visits, one should consider alternative diagnoses."*

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Final Clinical Algorithm: From Test to Treatment**

                              ### 🔄 **Step 1: Choose the Right Test**
                              - If **no contraindications** → **Dix-Hallpike**
                              - If **neck pain/extension issue** → **Modified Dix-Hallpike or Sidelying**
                              - If **equivocal** → **Repeat with different variant**

                              ### 🔄 **Step 2: Confirm Diagnosis**
                              - **Torsional-upbeating nystagmus** = **posterior canal BPPV**
                              - **Re-test after maneuver** to confirm resolution

                              ### 🔄 **Step 3: Choose the Right CRM**
                              - **Healthy patient** → **Modified Epley**
                              - **Cervical issues** → **Li Maneuver**
                              - **Obese/immobile** → **Semont Plus**
                              - **Failed Epley** → **Semont Plus or Li**

                              ### 🔄 **Step 4: Re-test and Progress**
                              - **Negative re-test** → proceed to **VORx1, FGA, home program**
                              - **Positive re-test** → **repeat CRM or consider apogeotropic conversion**

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Do not recommend postprocedural postural restrictions."*  
                              > → Patient can **sleep in any position** after treatment.

                              ---

                              ## ✅ **Conclusion: Precision in Testing and Treatment**

                              You are not just doing tests and maneuvers — you are **matching the right test to the patient’s safety and anatomy**, and **selecting the right treatment based on the test result and clinical context**.

                              Every decision is **evidence-based**, **patient-centered**, and **mechanically precise**.

                              When you walk into that practical exam, you won’t just say:
                              > “I’ll do Epley.”

                              You’ll say:
                              > “I performed a **Dix-Hallpike** and observed **right torsional-upbeating nystagmus**, confirming **right posterior canal BPPV**. Given the patient’s **cervical spondylosis**, I chose the **Li maneuver** to avoid neck extension. After treatment, I re-tested with a **negative Dix-Hallpike**, and initiated **VORx1 exercises** at 20–35 min/day.”

                              And that’s what makes you an expert.

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Part 1: Choosing Among Horizontal Canal Positional Tests (V.HC-BPPV-PT.1–3)**

                              You do **not** perform these tests randomly. You follow a **structured, evidence-based sequence** to **maximize diagnostic accuracy** and **minimize patient discomfort**.

                              From **NM.txt**:  
                              > *"It is best to perform the horizontal canal BPPV tests in the following order:  
                              > 1. Bow and Lean  
                              > 2. Sit to Supine  
                              > 3. Roll Test"*

                              Why this order? Let’s break it down.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **V.HC-BPPV-PT.3. Bow and Lean Test – First in Sequence**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Bow and Lean Test" is listed as the first test in the recommended sequence.*

                              #### ✅ **Purpose**:  
                              To **differentiate geotropic from apogeotropic BPPV** by assessing **nystagmus direction during pitch-plane head movements**.

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It**:
                              - As the **first test** in the horizontal canal workup
                              - When **Roll Test is inconclusive**
                              - To **confirm cupulolithiasis** (apogeotropic)

                              #### 🔹 **Procedure**:
                              1. Patient sits upright
                              2. **Bow forward** (flex head 30–60°) → observe for nystagmus
                              3. **Lean back** (extend head 30–60°) → observe for nystagmus

                              #### 🔹 **Interpretation**:

                              | BPPV Type | Bow (Flexion) | Lean (Extension) | Affected Side |
                              |----------|---------------|------------------|--------------|
                              | **Geotropic (Canalithiasis)** | Nystagmus **away from affected ear** | Nystagmus **toward affected ear** | Opposite to nystagmus direction |
                              | **Apogeotropic (Cupulolithiasis)** | Nystagmus **toward affected ear** | Nystagmus **away from affected ear** | Same as nystagmus direction |

                              > 📌 **NM.txt & UpRuperta.txt Connection**:  
                              > *"Table 2. Additional tests to determine side of involvement in horizontal SCC BPPV"*  
                              > This table provides the **gold standard for interpretation**.

                              #### 💡 **Clinical Pearl**:  
                              The **Bow and Lean Test** helps you **avoid misdiagnosing apogeotropic BPPV as geotropic**, which would lead to **wrong treatment**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **V.HC-BPPV-PT.1. Long Sit to Supine (Sit to Supine Test)**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Sit to supine test" is used to assess for horizontal canal BPPV.*

                              #### ✅ **Purpose**:  
                              To **provoke nystagmus without full side-lying**, useful when the **Roll Test is contraindicated** or **equivocal**.

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It**:
                              - Patient has **cervical spine limitations**
                              - Cannot tolerate **full side-lying positions**
                              - Used as a **screening test** before Roll Test

                              #### 🔹 **Procedure**:
                              1. Patient sits in long sitting, head flexed 20–30°
                              2. Rapidly lower to supine (head remains flexed)
                              3. Observe for **horizontal nystagmus**

                              #### 🔹 **Interpretation**:
                              - **Nystagmus beats AWAY from affected ear** → indicates **apogeotropic BPPV**
                              - **No nystagmus** → does not rule out BPPV

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Sit to Supine Test: Away from side of involvement" in apogeotropic BPPV*

                              #### ❌ **Limitations**:
                              - Less sensitive than Roll Test
                              - May not provoke nystagmus in mild cases

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **V.HC-BPPV-PT.2. Roll Test (Pagnini-McClure) – The Gold Standard**

                              > **NM.txt**: *"Roll Test (Pagnini-McClure Roll Test)" is the primary diagnostic test for HC-BPPV.*

                              #### ✅ **Purpose**:  
                              To **definitively diagnose horizontal canal BPPV** and **determine affected side** based on **nystagmus intensity and direction**.

                              #### ✅ **When to Use It**:
                              - After **Bow and Lean** and **Sit to Supine**
                              - When **Dix-Hallpike is negative** but positional vertigo persists
                              - First-line test for suspected HC-BPPV

                              #### 🔹 **Procedure**:
                              1. Patient supine, head elevated 30°
                              2. Rapidly roll head 90° to **right** → observe for 30 sec
                              3. Return to midline → wait 30 sec
                              4. Rapidly roll head 90° to **left** → observe for 30 sec

                              #### 🔹 **Interpretation**:

                              | Finding | Interpretation |
                              |--------|----------------|
                              | **Geotropic Nystagmus** (beats **toward undermost ear**) | **Canalithiasis** |
                              | **Apogeotropic Nystagmus** (beats **away from undermost ear**) | **Cupulolithiasis** |
                              | **More intense on one side** | In **geotropic**, **worse side = affected side** |
                              | **Less intense on one side** | In **apogeotropic**, **less intense side = affected side** |

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"The patient should only have vertigo or nystagmus if the right ear is involved with the test when the person lays to the right."*

                              #### 💡 **Memory Aid**:
                              - **G**eotropic = **G**ood (worse) side is **affected**
                              - **A**pogeotropic = **A**ffected side is the **less intense** one

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Summary: Why This Order Matters**

                              | Test | Why First? | What It Tells You |
                              |------|-----------|-------------------|
                              | **1. Bow and Lean** | Non-invasive, no side-lying | Differentiates **geotropic vs. apogeotropic** |
                              | **2. Sit to Supine** | Moderate provocation | Screens for **apogeotropic** |
                              | **3. Roll Test** | Most provocative, definitive | Confirms **side and type** |

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Make sure to write down the findings in each position. You may not see anything with the bow and lean or long sit to supine tests."*  
                              > → But if you **do**, it’s **diagnostically critical**.

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Part 2: From Test Findings to Treatment – Choosing the Right CRM (VI.HC-CCRM.1–5)**

                              Now that you’ve diagnosed the **type and side**, you must choose the **correct repositioning maneuver**.

                              From **NM.txt**:  
                              > *"Horizontal canal BPPV CRM: Geotropic: Gufoni or Li Quick; Apogeotropic: Kim Maneuver or Gufoni"*

                              Let’s break it down by **type**.

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Geotropic HC-BPPV (Canalithiasis) → Otoconia Freely Floating in Long Arm**

                              #### ✅ **Positive Findings**:
                              - **Roll Test**: Nystagmus beats **toward undermost ear**
                              - **Intensity**: **Worse on affected side**
                              - **Fatigability**: Yes (canaliths settle)
                              - **Bow and Lean**: Nystagmus **away from affected ear** during bow

                              #### ✅ **Recommended Maneuvers**:
                              1. **HC-CCRM.1. Barbecue Maneuver (Lempert Roll)**  
                                 - Rotates patient 360° in bed
                                 - Moves debris **out of long arm** into utricle
                                 - Effective but **nauseating** — not first choice for frail patients

                              2. **HC-CCRM.2. Gufoni Maneuver (for Canalithiasis)**  
                                 - Patient lies on **affected side**, head turned **upward 30°**
                                 - Holds 2 min → rolls to back → sits up
                                 - **First-line** for geotropic (NM.txt)

                              3. **HC-CCRM.3. Li Quick Maneuver**  
                                 - Rapid lateral throw from **unaffected to affected side**
                                 - Uses **inertial force** to dislodge debris
                                 - Fast, but **high velocity** — use caution

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Gufoni maneuver for geotropic nystagmus (first choice)"*

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**: Kim Maneuver — designed for **cupulolithiasis**

                              ---

                              ### 🔹 **Apogeotropic HC-BPPV (Cupulolithiasis) → Otoconia Adhered to Cupula**

                              #### ✅ **Positive Findings**:
                              - **Roll Test**: Nystagmus beats **away from undermost ear**
                              - **Intensity**: **Less intense on affected side**
                              - **Persistence**: Non-fatiguing, may last >1 min
                              - **Bow and Lean**: Nystagmus **toward affected ear** during bow

                              #### ✅ **Recommended Maneuvers**:
                              1. **HC-CCRM.5. Kim Maneuver (First Choice)**  
                                 - Patient lies on **unaffected side**
                                 - Head extended 30° → holds 2 min
                                 - Rolls to back → then to **affected side** → sits up
                                 - Uses gravity to **detach otoconia from cupula**
                                 - **Supported by RCTs** (Kim et al., 2017)

                              2. **HC-CCRM.4. Gufoni Maneuver (for Cupulolithiasis)**  
                                 - Patient lies on **affected side**
                                 - Head turned **downward 30°** (toward floor)
                                 - Holds 2 min → rolls to back → sits up
                                 - Forces cupula to **swing away** from canal
                                 - Less effective than Kim, but commonly used

                              > 📌 **NM.txt & UpRuperta.txt**: *"Kim maneuver for ageotropic; Gufoni for ageotropic nystagmus"*

                              #### ❌ **Do NOT Use**: Barbecue or Li Quick — may **worsen** cupulolithiasis

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Summary: From Test to Treatment – Clinical Decision Table**

                              | Test Finding | Interpretation | Affected Side | Mechanism | Recommended CRM |
                              |-------------|----------------|---------------|-----------|------------------|
                              | **Roll Test**: Nystagmus beats **right** when **right ear down**, **more intense** | Geotropic HC-BPPV | **Right** | Canalithiasis | **Gufoni (right side)** or **Barbecue** |
                              | **Roll Test**: Nystagmus beats **left** when **right ear down**, **less intense** | Apogeotropic HC-BPPV | **Right** | Cupulolithiasis | **Kim (right side)** or **Gufoni (right side, head down)** |
                              | **Bow and Lean**: Nystagmus **toward right** during bow | Apogeotropic HC-BPPV | **Right** | Cupulolithiasis | **Kim** or **Gufoni** |
                              | **Sit to Supine**: Nystagmus beats **left** | Apogeotropic HC-BPPV | **Right** | Cupulolithiasis | **Kim** or **Gufoni** |
                              | **Roll Test negative, Bow and Lean positive** | Apogeotropic HC-BPPV | Based on nystagmus | Cupulolithiasis | **Kim** or **Gufoni** |

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Biomechanics Deep Dive: What Happens to the Otoconia?**

                              ### 🔹 **Geotropic BPPV (Canalithiasis)**
                              - Otoconia float in the **long arm** of the horizontal canal
                              - When affected ear is down, gravity pulls debris **away from cupula** → **ampullofugal flow** → **excitation** → nystagmus **toward ground**
                              - **Gufoni Maneuver**: Forces debris **out of canal** by aligning it with utricle

                              ### 🔹 **Apogeotropic BPPV (Cupulolithiasis)**
                              - Otoconia are **stuck to the cupula**, making it heavier
                              - When affected ear is **up**, the cupula is **pulled downward** → **ampullopetal deflection** → **excitation** → nystagmus **away from ground**
                              - **Kim Maneuver**: On unaffected side, head extension **increases gravitational pull** on otoconia, helping them **detach**

                              > 💡 **Key Insight**:  
                              > In **apogeotropic**, the **cupula is deflected even when the affected ear is up** — that’s why nystagmus is **less intense** when it’s down.

                              ---

                              ## 🔁 **Final Clinical Algorithm: Horizontal Canal BPPV Workup**

                              ### 🔄 **Step 1: Order of Testing**
                              1. **Bow and Lean** → differentiate geotropic vs. apogeotropic
                              2. **Sit to Supine** → screen for apogeotropic
                              3. **Roll Test** → confirm diagnosis and side

                              ### 🔄 **Step 2: Interpret Findings**
                              - **Geotropic**: Nystagmus **toward undermost ear**, **worse on affected side**
                              - **Apogeotropic**: Nystagmus **away from undermost ear**, **less intense on affected side**

                              ### 🔄 **Step 3: Choose CRM**
                              | Type | Maneuver | Why |
                              |------|--------|-----|
                              | **Geotropic** | **Gufoni (affected side)** | First-line, high success rate |
                              | **Geotropic** | **Barbecue or Li Quick** | Alternatives if Gufoni fails |
                              | **Apogeotropic** | **Kim Maneuver** | Detaches otoconia from cupula |
                              | **Apogeotropic** | **Gufoni (affected side, head down)** | Alternative if Kim not feasible |

                              ### 🔄 **Step 4: Re-test**
                              - Perform **Roll Test again** after maneuver
                              - If **positive**, repeat or switch maneuver
                              - If **negative**, proceed to **VORx1, FGA, home program**

                              > 📌 **NM.txt**: *"Treating with repeated canalith repositioning maneuvers is superior to treating with one maneuver only."*

                              ---

                              ## ✅ **Conclusion: Precision in Diagnosis and Treatment**

                              You are not just doing tests and maneuvers — you are **matching the right test to the patient**, **interpreting nystagmus with precision**, and **selecting the correct CRM based on biomechanics and evidence**.

                              When you walk into that practical exam, you won’t just say:
                              > “I’ll do Gufoni.”

                              You’ll say:
                              > “The **Roll Test** showed **apogeotropic nystagmus**, beating **away from the right ear** when right ear was down, and **less intense on the right**, confirming **right apogeotropic HC-BPPV (cupulolithiasis)**. I performed the **Kim maneuver** to detach the otoconia from the cupula. After treatment, the **Roll Test was negative**, and I initiated **VORx1 exercises**.”

                              And that’s what makes you an expert.

                  .Patient Case 1 Γ(Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV))
                     🎯 Simulation Objective:
                     ## 🧪 SIMULATED PATIENT CASE: "Ruperta"

                     > Name: Ruperta M.  
                     > Age: 72 years  
                     > Setting: Outpatient Neurological Rehabilitation Clinic  
                     > Referral: "Intermittent vertigo with position changes"  
                     > Chart Review Summary (from UpRuperta.txt & NM.txt context):
                     > - Episodes of vertigo when bending down and standing up  
                     > - Lasts less than 30 seconds, resolves with stillness  
                     > - No hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurological symptoms  
                     > - Dix-Hallpike Maneuver:
                     >   - Right side: Negative  
                     >   - Left side: Positive  
                     >   - Nystagmus: 3-second latency, 15-second duration, torsional upbeating toward the left ear, crescendo-decrescendo pattern  
                     >   - Accompanied by vertigo  
                     > - PMH: HTN, osteoarthritis  
                     > - Meds: Lisinopril  
                     > - Social: Lives alone, walks dog daily, fell once last month  
                     > - Prior Level of Function (PLF): Independent ambulator, community walker

                     ---

                     ## 1º. WHAT WOULD YOU ASK IN THE INTERVIEW?

                     Let’s start with History, which is the first component of the Neurologic PT Examination.

                     ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: Why Are We Asking This?

                     The interview is not just about symptoms — it's about forming clinical hypotheses and ruling out red flags.

                     Dizziness can come from:
                     - Peripheral vestibular (inner ear): BPPV, vestibular neuritis
                     - Central vestibular (brainstem/cerebellum): stroke, MS
                     - Cardiovascular: orthostatic hypotension
                     - Medication side effects
                     - Cervicogenic or psychological causes

                     So our questions help us:
                     - Localize the system involved
                     - Rule out dangerous conditions
                     - Establish baseline function and safety

                     Also, per your feedback, you missed social history, fall history, and prior level of function (PLF) — these are critical for safety and goal setting.

                     ---

                     ### ✅ STRUCTURED INTERVIEW QUESTIONS

                     We’ll follow the Neurological Evaluation Lab Worksheet framework.

                     ---

                     #### A. History of Present Illness (HPI) – Chief Complaint: “I feel dizzy when I move my head”

                     Ask:

                     1. Onset:  
                        - “When did this start?”  
                        - Why? Sudden onset suggests peripheral vestibular (e.g., neuritis). Gradual = degenerative or medication.

                     2. Triggers:  
                        - “Does anything bring it on? Like rolling over in bed, looking up, bending down?”  
                        - Why? Positional triggers = BPPV. Movement-related = vestibular hypofunction.

                     3. Duration:  
                        - “How long does each episode last?”  
                        - Why? Seconds = BPPV. Minutes to hours = vestibular migraine or TIA. Constant = neuritis or CNS lesion.

                     4. Quality:  
                        - “Is it spinning (vertigo), lightheadedness, or unsteadiness?”  
                        - Why? True vertigo (room spinning) → vestibular system. Lightheadedness → cardiovascular or anxiety.

                     5. Associated Symptoms:  
                        - “Any hearing loss, ringing in ears, nausea, headache, double vision, weakness?”  
                        - Why? Hearing changes → Meniere’s. Neurologic symptoms → central lesion.

                     6. Course:  
                        - “Is it getting better, worse, or coming and going?”  
                        - Why? Improving = likely peripheral. Fluctuating = Meniere’s or migraine.

                     ---

                     #### B. Past Medical History (PMH)

                     Ask:
                     - “Any history of stroke, diabetes, Parkinson’s, ear infections?”  
                     - “Neck problems or head injuries?”  
                     - Why? These can mimic or contribute to dizziness.

                     ---

                     #### C. Medications & Allergies

                     - “What medications are you taking?”  
                     - Why? Antihypertensives → orthostatic hypotension. Benzodiazepines → dizziness.

                     ---

                     #### D. Social History & Prior Level of Function (PLF) ← YOU MISSED THIS LAST TIME

                     Ask:
                     - “Do you live alone? Do you have stairs at home?”  
                     - “Before this started, could you walk independently? Do you drive?”  
                     - “Have you fallen? How many times? Any injuries?”  
                     - “What do you enjoy doing?”  
                     - Why? This tells us about safety risks, home environment, and functional goals. Falls history is a RED FLAG.

                     ---

                     #### E. Patient Goals

                     - “What would you like to be able to do again?”  
                     - “Are you afraid of falling?”  
                     - Why? Guides treatment planning and outcome measures (e.g., Dizziness Handicap Inventory).

                     ---

                     ### 🧩 CLINICAL REASONING MAP: Where Does This Fit?

                     All these questions are part of Step 2: History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS).

                     This step helps us:
                     - Form hypotheses (e.g., “This sounds like BPPV”)
                     - Decide what systems to test next
                     - Identify red flags (e.g., sudden vertigo + ataxia = possible stroke)
                     - Establish baseline function and safety concerns

                     > 🔁 Reminder: The Review of Systems (ROS) is a screening tool to rule in/out system involvement. If positive, we do a further detailed examination.

                     ---

                     ## 2º. WHAT WOULD YOU PRIORITIZE IN THE NEUROLOGIC EXAM?

                     Now, based on the history, we prioritize components of the neurologic exam.

                     From the chart:  
                     > “Episodes of vertigo with position changes, lasting <30 sec, torsional upbeating nystagmus on left Dix-Hallpike”

                     👉 This is classic Left Posterior Canal BPPV — a peripheral vestibular disorder.

                     But we must rule out central causes and assess safety.

                     ---

                     ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Neurologic Exam Framework

                     The exam follows a hierarchical order:

                     1. Mental Status → Is the patient alert and able to participate?
                     2. Cranial Nerves → Especially II, III, IV, VI, VIII for oculomotor and vestibular function
                     3. Sensory → Is proprioception intact? (dorsal column)
                     4. Motor → Strength, tone, coordination
                     5. Balance & Coordination → Static, dynamic, walking
                     6. Functional Skills → Sit-to-stand, gait, transfers

                     > ⚠️ Why this order? Because higher-level systems affect lower-level ones. If a patient is confused or has gaze palsy, balance testing may be invalid.

                     ---

                     ### ✅ PRIORITIZED EXAM COMPONENTS FOR THIS PATIENT

                     We’ll go through each, explaining why, what we’re looking for, and how it fits into the bigger picture.

                     ---

                     #### 2.a. History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS)

                     Already done above.

                     Now, during observation:
                     - Watch how she enters the clinic: unsteady? Using furniture?
                     - Does she avoid head movements?
                     - Why? Natural movement reveals compensatory strategies and fear of movement.

                     ---

                     #### 2.b. Sensory Exam

                     We focus on systems relevant to balance:

                     1. Light Touch – Screen dermatomes (e.g., L5-S1)  
                        - Why? Rule out peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy.

                     2. Proprioception (Joint Position Sense) – Big toe up/down  
                        - Why? This tests the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway. Impaired proprioception → poor balance, especially in dark.

                     > 🔄 Compare: In BPPV, proprioception is intact. In bilateral vestibulopathy, it may be relied upon heavily.

                     ---

                     #### 3.c. Balance Exam

                     This is critical for dizziness.

                     Breakdown:
                     - Static Standing Balance: Sensory orientation & reactive control
                     - Dynamic Standing Balance: Self-generated control
                     - Walking Balance

                     Use standardized tools from the Core Set of Outcome Measures:
                     - Berg Balance Scale (BBS) – Static and dynamic balance
                     - Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) – Walking with head turns, eyes closed, etc.
                     - Mini-BESTest – Specifically assesses balance control systems

                     > 🔍 Why these? Because they’re evidence-based, valid, and responsive to change in vestibular patients.

                     ---

                     #### 4.d. Mental Status Exam

                     Quick screen:
                     - Alertness: Is she awake and responsive?
                     - Orientation: Person, place, time
                     - Attention: Can she follow 2-step commands?
                     - Why? To ensure she can participate in vestibular rehab. Cognitive impairment changes treatment approach.

                     ---

                     #### 5.e. Motor Exam

                     Key elements:

                     1. Muscle Mass – Any atrophy? (e.g., from inactivity)
                     2. ROM – Cervical rotation? Limited ROM may cause cervicogenic dizziness.
                     3. Tone – Normal? Spasticity suggests UMN lesion.
                     4. Strength – Manual muscle testing (MMT) of legs and neck
                        - Why? Weakness contributes to imbalance.
                     5. Motor Control – Can she isolate head movements?
                     6. Involuntary Movements – Tremor? Nystagmus?

                     > 🔄 Compare: In BPPV, strength and tone are normal. In Parkinson’s, you’d see rigidity and bradykinesia.

                     ---

                     #### 6.f. Functional Skills Exam and Movement Analysis

                     Observe:
                     - Sit-to-Stand: Smooth? Uses arms?  
                     - Transfers: Needs help?  
                     - Walking: Wide base? Head stiff?  
                     - Stairs: Can she do them?

                     Use Movement Analysis Worksheet to note:
                     - Initiation delay
                     - Trunk stiffness
                     - Head-trunk dissociation
                     - Step length asymmetry

                     > 🔄 Compare: In BPPV, gait is often cautious but symmetric. In cerebellar ataxia, it’s wide-based and irregular.

                     ---

                     #### 7.g. Cranial Nerve Integrity Exam

                     Prioritize:
                     - CN II (Optic): Visual acuity, visual fields  
                     - CN III, IV, VI: Extraocular movements (H-test), saccades, smooth pursuit, convergence  
                     - CN VIII (Vestibulocochlear): Hearing (whisper test), VOR (HIT), nystagmus

                     > 🔍 Why? To assess oculomotor and vestibular function — central to dizziness.

                     ---

                     #### 8.h. Coordination Exam

                     - Finger-to-Nose (FTN): Check for dysmetria (past-pointing) → cerebellar lesion
                     - Heel-to-Shin (HTS): Same
                     - Rapid Alternating Movements (RAM): Pronation/supination → dysdiadochokinesia

                     > 🔄 Compare: In BPPV, coordination is normal. In central vertigo, it’s impaired.

                     ---

                     ## 3º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT TO RULE OUT BPPV

                     Now, we rule out BPPV using positional testing.

                     ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: What Is BPPV?

                     - Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is a peripheral vestibular disorder.
                     - Caused by otoconia (calcium crystals) in semicircular canals.
                     - Most common: Posterior canal BPPV → geotropic torsional upbeating nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike.

                     > 🔄 Compare:  
                     > - Horizontal canal BPPV → horizontal nystagmus  
                     > - Central positional nystagmus → downbeating, no latency, no fatigue

                     ---

                     ### ✅ TESTS TO RULE OUT BPPV

                     1. Dix-Hallpike Maneuver  
                        - Purpose: Diagnose posterior canal BPPV  
                        - How:  
                          - Sit → quickly lay back with head 20° below table, turned 45° to one side  
                          - Feet must be on the ground or supported ← SAFETY ISSUE FROM YOUR FEEDBACK  
                          - Observe for nystagmus and vertigo  
                        - Positive if:  
                          - Latency (1–5 sec delay)  
                          - Rotational (torsional) + upbeating nystagmus  
                          - Fatigues with repetition  
                          - Vertigo matches symptoms

                     2. Supine Roll Test  
                        - Purpose: Diagnose horizontal canal BPPV  
                        - How: Lie on back → rapidly roll head 90° left/right  
                        - Positive if: horizontal nystagmus, beats toward lower ear (geotropic) or upper ear (ageotropic)

                     > ⚠️ Safety: Feet on ground or supported during all tests. You were marked down for this.

                     ---

                     ## 4º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT (General)

                     Now, broader vestibular and oculomotor screening:

                     ### ✅ VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening)

                     From your files: VOMS includes:
                     1. Smooth Pursuits – Follow finger slowly side to side  
                        - Abnormal: Saccadic (jumpy) tracking → cerebellar/brainstem
                     2. Saccades – Rapid shift between two targets  
                        - Abnormal: Overshoot/undershoot → frontal lobe, basal ganglia
                     3. Near Point Convergence – Finger moves toward nose  
                        - Abnormal: Double vision before 5–7 cm → midbrain or CN III
                     4. VOR (Head Impulse Test)  
                        - How: Small, quick head turn left/right while patient fixates on your nose  
                        - Positive: Catch-up saccade → ipsilateral vestibular hypofunction
                        - Why? Tests high-frequency VOR — if impaired, patient can’t stabilize gaze during walking
                     5. Positional Testing – Already done (Dix-Hallpike)

                     > 🔄 Compare:  
                     > - BPPV: Positive Dix-Hallpike, normal VOR  
                     > - Vestibular Neuritis: Abnormal VOR, spontaneous nystagmus, negative Dix-Hallpike

                     ---

                     ## 5º. WHAT TREATMENT WOULD YOU PROVIDE?

                     ### ✅ For BPPV: Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers

                     - Posterior Canal BPPV → Epley Maneuver  
                     - Horizontal Canal BPPV → Barbecue (Lempert) Roll

                     > 🔍 Why? These use gravity to move otoconia out of the canal.

                     Epley Steps:
                     1. Sit → turn head 45° affected side
                     2. Lay back, head 20° below table
                     3. Wait 30 sec (nystagmus fatigues)
                     4. Turn head 90° to opposite side
                     5. Turn body 90°, face down
                     6. Sit up

                     > ⚠️ Feet on ground during transitions ← SAFETY

                     ---

                     ## 6º. HOW WOULD YOU ASSESS DIFFICULTY?

                     Use objective and subjective measures:

                     - Symptoms: Rate dizziness/nausea 0–10 before/during/after
                     - Vital Signs: BP, HR (especially if orthostatic)
                     - RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion): 0–10
                     - Functional Tests: Repeat FGA or BBS to track progress
                     - DHI (Dizziness Handicap Inventory): Patient-reported disability

                     > 🔁 You were marked down for not measuring symptoms to progress/regress treatment.

                     ---

                     ## 7º. HOW WOULD YOU PROGRESS/REGRESS THE TREATMENT?

                     ### 🔁 Progression:
                     - Increase head movements during gait
                     - Add dual-task (walk and talk)
                     - Reduce base of support (tandem stance)
                     - Add unstable surfaces (foam)
                     - Increase speed of movements

                     ### 🔁 Regression:
                     - Slow down head movements
                     - Use visual cues
                     - Reduce duration
                     - Perform seated first
                     - Provide hand support

                     > 📊 Use symptom response to guide:  
                     > - < 3/10 → progress  
                     > - > 5/10 → regress or stop

                     2. Home Program:  
                        - Brandt-Daroff Exercises (if Epley not fully effective)  
                        - Avoid sleeping on affected side for 48 hours  
                        - Move slowly with head turns

                     3. Safety:  
                        - Use a cane if unsteady  
                        - Install grab bars in bathroom  
                        - Sit down when dizzy

                     4. Red Flags:  
                        - “If you get new weakness, slurred speech, or severe headache — go to ER.”

                     > ⚠️ You were marked 1/5 on education — be specific and clear.

                        ## 🧪 PATIENT CASE: "Ruperta M."

                        > Age: 72  
                        > Chief Complaint: “I get dizzy when I bend down to tie my shoes or roll over in bed.”  
                        > Duration: Episodes last less than 30 seconds; resolve when still  
                        > No associated symptoms: No hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, weakness, or numbness  
                        > Dix-Hallpike Maneuver:  
                        > - Right side: Negative  
                        > - Left side: Positive  
                        >   - Latency: 3 seconds  
                        >   - Duration: 15 seconds

                        >   - Pattern: Crescendo-decrescendo
