                           ## 6º. HOW WOULD YOU ASSESS DIFFICULTY?

                           Use objective and subjective measures:

                           - Symptoms: Rate dizziness/nausea 0–10 before/during/after
                           - Vital Signs: BP, HR (especially if orthostatic)
                           - RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion): 0–10
                           - Functional Tests: Repeat FGA or BBS to track progress
                           - DHI (Dizziness Handicap Inventory): Patient-reported disability

                           > 🔁 You were marked down for not measuring symptoms to progress/regress treatment.

                           ---

                           ## 7º. HOW WOULD YOU PROGRESS/REGRESS THE TREATMENT?

                           ### 🔁 Progression:
                           - Increase head movement speed
                           - Add dual-task (walk and talk)
                           - Reduce base of support (tandem stance)
                           - Add unstable surfaces (foam)
                           - Increase complexity of gait (obstacles, stairs)

                           ### 🔁 Regression:
                           - Slow down head movements
                           - Use visual cues
                           - Reduce duration
                           - Perform seated first
                           - Provide hand support

                           > 📊 Use symptom response to guide:  
                           > - < 3/10 → progress  
                           > - > 5/10 → regress or stop

                           ## 🧪 PATIENT CASE 14  
                           ### Γ(Bilateral Vestibulopathy)

                           This is a critical and high-yield case — bilateral vestibulopathy (BVP), also known as bilateral vestibular hypofunction (BVH), is a chronic, disabling condition that profoundly impacts balance, gait, and quality of life.

                           Unlike unilateral vestibular disorders (e.g., vestibular neuritis, BPPV), where the brain can compensate by relying on the intact side, bilateral vestibulopathy means both sides of the vestibular system are impaired. There is no asymmetry to drive vertigo, but there is severe instability because the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and vestibulospinal reflex (VSR) are both compromised.

                           This case will challenge your ability to:
                           - Recognize the absence of vertigo but presence of imbalance and oscillopsia
                           - Differentiate BVP from central ataxia and sensory ataxia
                           - Perform and interpret clinical tests like HIT, DVA, and mCTSIB
                           - Rule out central causes (e.g., cerebellar degeneration, MS)
                           - Initiate appropriate vestibular rehabilitation focused on substitution and sensory reweighting
                           - Provide clear patient education about lifestyle adaptations and safety

                           We’ll follow your exact learning framework:
                           - Start with Medical Diagnosis (MDx) and Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx) — stated upfront
                           - Provide big picture context
                           - Walk through interview, exam, tests, treatment, progression, education
                           - Emphasize why we do (or don’t do) each step
                           - Compare with other conditions (e.g., unilateral vestibulopathy, BPPV, cerebellar ataxia)
                           - Address your past exam feedback (e.g., safety, PLF, motor exam, explanation)

                           Let’s begin.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ Medical Diagnosis (MDx):  
                           Bilateral Vestibulopathy (Bilateral Vestibular Hypofunction)

                           ### ✅ Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx):  
                           1. Impaired postural control associated with bilateral vestibular hypofunction  
                           2. Impaired gaze stability associated with vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) dysfunction  
                           3. Impaired functional mobility associated with dynamic imbalance and movement-provoked oscillopsia

                           > 🔍 Why these PT diagnoses?  
                           > - #1 is the primary PT diagnosis — the patient has poor balance due to loss of vestibular input on both sides.  
                           > - #2 reflects that the VOR is impaired, leading to oscillopsia (bouncing vision) during walking or head movements.  
                           > - #3 is secondary but critical: the patient avoids movement due to fear, which limits function.

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In unilateral vestibulopathy, PT Dx includes vertigo and asymmetry — here, no vertigo, but worse imbalance.  
                           > - In sensory ataxia, proprioception is impaired — here, proprioception is intact, but integration is poor.

                           > 📌 Key Point: The PT diagnosis reflects the movement system impairment, not the medical diagnosis. But the treatment approach changes dramatically based on the underlying pathology.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: Where Does This Case Fit?

                           All vertigo and imbalance cases fall into two main categories:

                           ### 🌐 1. Vestibular System Disorders
                              - Peripheral (inner ear): BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, bilateral vestibulopathy
                              - Central (brain): Stroke, MS, tumor

                           This is peripheral, specifically bilateral vestibulopathy — a chronic vestibular syndrome caused by reduced or absent function of both vestibular organs/nerves.

                           #### 🔹 Key Features of Bilateral Vestibulopathy:
                           - No vertigo (no asymmetry)
                           - Chronic imbalance, worse with movement
                           - Oscillopsia (visual blurring with head movement or walking)
                           - Worsening in dark or on uneven surfaces
                           - Positive Head Impulse Test (HIT) bilaterally
                           - Abnormal Dynamic Visual Acuity (DVA)

                           > - If you expect vertigo, you’ll miss the diagnosis.  
                           > - If you see downbeat nystagmus or dysmetria, suspect central cause.  
                           > - If you see absent proprioception, think sensory ataxia.

                           Our job is to:
                           1. Confirm it’s bilateral vestibulopathy
                           2. Rule out central causes (e.g., cerebellar degeneration, MS)
                           3. Initiate vestibular rehab focused on substitution and sensory reweighting
                           4. Educate the patient about safety, assistive devices, and lifestyle changes

                           ### ✅ STRUCTURED INTERVIEW QUESTIONS

                           #### A. History of Present Illness (HPI)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Onset: “When did this start?” | Acute vs. chronic process | Gradual onset → BVP. Sudden → stroke or neuritis | Helps differentiate BVP from other conditions |
                           | Quality: “Is it spinning, lightheaded, or unsteady?” | True vertigo vs. presyncope | No spinning → rules out BPPV. Unsteadiness → BVP | Mislabeling dizziness leads to wrong testing pathway |
                           | Triggers: “Does anything make it worse?” | Movement, lighting, surface | Worse in dark/uneven → BVP. Positional → BPPV | If you don’t ask, you might miss the key diagnostic clue |
                           | Associated Symptoms: “Any oscillopsia, hearing loss, headache, weakness?” | Cochlear or CNS involvement | Oscillopsia → BVP. Hearing loss → labyrinthitis. Weakness → stroke | Missing neurologic symptoms could delay life-saving referral |
                           | Course: “Is it getting better, worse, or coming and going?” | Progression pattern | Worsening → central lesion or progressive BVP | Helps determine prognosis and urgency |

                           ---

                           #### B. Past Medical History (PMH)

                           Ask:
                           - “Any history of stroke, diabetes, Parkinson’s, ear infections?”  
                           - “Neck problems or head injuries?”  
                           - Why? These can mimic or contribute to dizziness.

                           > In this case: History of TB + ototoxic meds → classic cause of BVP.

                           ---

                           #### C. Medications & Allergies

                           - “What medications are you taking?”  
                           - Why? Ototoxic drugs → cause BVP. Vestibular suppressants → delay compensation.

                           > In this case: Streptomycin and isoniazid → known ototoxins.

                           ---

                           #### D. Social History, Fall History, and Prior Level of Function (PLF) ← YOU MISSED THIS LAST TIME

                           | Question | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Do you live alone or with someone?” | Safety, home environment, support system | Living with daughter → may reduce fall risk | Without this, you can’t assess safety or design safe HEP |
                           | “Before this started, could you walk independently? Do you drive?” | PLF = baseline for goals | Was he independent? Driving? Climbing stairs? | You can’t measure progress without knowing baseline |
                           | “Have you fallen? How many times? Any injuries?” | Red flag for injury risk | “Have you fallen?” → yes, twice | Falls = high risk; affects intervention choices and safety |
                           | “What do you enjoy doing?” | Patient-centered goals | “I walk daily” → functional goal | Guides treatment planning |

                           ### 🧩 CLINICAL REASONING MAP: Where Does This Fit?

                           All these questions are part of Step 2: History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS).

                           This step helps us:
                           - Form hypotheses (e.g., “This sounds like bilateral vestibulopathy”)
                           - Decide what systems to test next
                           - Identify red flags (e.g., sudden vertigo + ataxia = possible stroke)
                           - Establish baseline function and safety concerns

                           > 🔁 Reminder: The Review of Systems (ROS) is a screening tool to rule in/out system involvement. If positive, we do a further detailed examination.

                           ## 2º. WHAT WOULD YOU PRIORITIZE IN THE NEUROLOGIC EXAM?

                           Now, based on the history, we prioritize components of the neurologic exam.

                           From the chart:  
                           > “Chronic imbalance, oscillopsia, bilateral HIT positive, DVA loss, mCTSIB Condition 4 failed”

                           👉 This is classic Bilateral Vestibulopathy — a peripheral vestibular disorder with bilateral involvement.

                           But we must rule out central causes and assess safety.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Neurologic Exam Framework

                           The exam follows a hierarchical order:

                           1. Mental Status → Is the patient alert and able to participate?
                           2. Cranial Nerves → Especially II, III, IV, VI, VIII for oculomotor and vestibular function
                           3. Sensory → Is proprioception intact? (dorsal column)
                           4. Motor → Strength, tone, coordination
                           5. Balance & Coordination → Static, dynamic, walking
                           6. Functional Skills → Sit-to-stand, gait, transfers

                           > ⚠️ Why this order? Because higher-level systems affect lower-level ones. If a patient is confused or has gaze palsy, balance testing may be invalid.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ PRIORITIZED EXAM COMPONENTS FOR THIS PATIENT

                           We’ll go through each, explaining why, what we’re looking for, and how it fits into the bigger picture.

                           ---

                           #### 2.a. History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS)

                           Already done above.

                           Now, during observation:
                           - Watch how he enters the clinic: wide-based gait? Using cane?
                           - Does he avoid walking in dim light?
                           - Why? Natural behavior reveals compensatory strategies and fear of movement.

                           ---

                           #### 2.b. Sensory Exam

                           We focus on systems relevant to balance:

                           1. Light Touch – Screen dermatomes (e.g., L5-S1)  
                              - Why? Rule out peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy.

                           2. Proprioception (Joint Position Sense) – Big toe up/down  
                              - Why? This tests the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway. Impaired proprioception → poor balance, especially in dark.

                           > 🔄 Compare: In BVP, proprioception is intact — imbalance is due to lack of vestibular input, not sensory loss.

                           ---

                           #### 3.c. Balance Exam

                           This is critical for dizziness.

                           Breakdown:
                           - Static Standing Balance: Sensory orientation & reactive control
                           - Dynamic Standing Balance: Self-generated control
                           - Walking Balance

                           Use standardized tools:
                           - Berg Balance Scale (BBS) – Static and dynamic balance
                           - Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) – Walking with head turns, eyes closed
                           - Mini-BESTest – Specifically assesses balance control systems
                           - mCTSIB – Conditions 1–4

                           > 🔍 Why these? Because they’re evidence-based, valid, and responsive to change in vestibular patients.

                           ---

                           #### 4.d. Mental Status Exam

                           Quick screen:
                           - Alertness: Is he awake and responsive?
                           - Orientation: Person, place, time
                           - Attention: Can he follow 2-step commands?
                           - Why? To ensure he can participate in vestibular rehab. Cognitive impairment changes treatment approach.

                           ---

                           #### 5.e. Motor Exam

                           Key elements:

                           1. Muscle Mass – Any atrophy? (e.g., from inactivity)
                           2. ROM – Cervical rotation? Limited ROM may cause cervicogenic dizziness.
                           3. Tone – Normal? Spasticity suggests UMN lesion.
                           4. Strength – Manual muscle testing (MMT) of legs and neck
                              - Why? Weakness contributes to imbalance.
                           5. Motor Control – Can he isolate head movements?
                           6. Involuntary Movements – Tremor? Nystagmus?

                           > 🔄 Compare: In BVP, strength and tone are normal. In Parkinson’s, you’d see rigidity and bradykinesia.

                           ---

                           #### 6.f. Functional Skills Exam and Movement Analysis

                           Observe:
                           - Sit-to-Stand: Smooth? Uses arms?  
                           - Transfers: Needs help?  
                           - Walking: Wide base? Head stiff?  
                           - Stairs: Can he do them?

                           Use Movement Analysis Worksheet to note:
                           - Initiation delay
                           - Trunk stiffness
                           - Head-trunk dissociation
                           - Step length asymmetry

                           > 🔄 Compare: In BVP, gait is wide-based, slow, cautious. In cerebellar ataxia, it’s irregular, staggering.

                           ---

                           #### 7.g. Cranial Nerve Integrity Exam

                           Prioritize:
                           - CN II (Optic): Visual acuity, visual fields  
                           - CN III, IV, VI: Extraocular movements (H-test), saccades, smooth pursuit, convergence  
                           - CN VIII (Vestibulocochlear): Hearing (whisper test), VOR (HIT), nystagmus

                           > 🔍 Why? To assess oculomotor and vestibular function — central to dizziness.

                           ---

                           #### 8.h. Coordination Exam

                           - Finger to nose
                           - Heel to shin
                           - Rapid alternating movement

                           > 🔄 Compare: In BVP, coordination is normal. In central vertigo, it’s impaired.

                           ---

                           ## 3º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT TO RULE OUT BPPV

                           Now, we rule out BPPV using positional testing.

                           ### ✅ TESTS TO RULE OUT BPPV

                           1. Dix-Hallpike Maneuver  
                              - Purpose: Diagnose posterior canal BPPV  
                              - How: Sit → quickly lay back, head 20° below table, turned 45° to one side  
                              - In this case: Negative bilaterally → rules out posterior canal BPPV

                           2. Supine Roll Test  
                              - Purpose: Diagnose horizontal canal BPPV  
                              - How: Lie on back → rapidly roll head 90° left/right  
                              - In this case: Negative bilaterally → rules out horizontal canal BPPV

                           > ⚠️ Safety: Feet on ground or supported during all tests. You were marked down for this.

                           ---

                           ## 4º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT (General)

                           Now, broader vestibular and oculomotor screening:

                           ### ✅ VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening)

                           From your files: VOMS includes:
                           1. Smooth Pursuits – Follow finger slowly side to side  
                              - Abnormal: Saccadic (jumpy) tracking → cerebellar/brainstem
                           2. Saccades – Rapid shift between two targets  
                              - Abnormal: Overshoot/undershoot → frontal lobe, basal ganglia
                           3. Near Point Convergence – Finger moves toward nose  
                              - Abnormal: Double vision before 5–7 cm → midbrain or CN III
                           4. VOR (Head Impulse Test)  
                              - How: Small, quick head turn left/right while patient fixates on your nose  
                              - Positive: Catch-up saccade bilaterally → bilateral vestibular hypofunction
                              - Why? Tests high-frequency VOR — if impaired, patient can’t stabilize gaze during walking
                           5. Positional Testing – Already done (Dix-Hallpike, Supine Roll)

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - BPPV: Positive Dix-Hallpike, normal VOR  
                           > - Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Abnormal VOR bilaterally, no vertigo, oscillopsia

                           ---

                           ## 5º. WHAT TREATMENT WOULD YOU PROVIDE?

                           ### ✅ For Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT)

                           - VOR Substitution Exercises (e.g., gaze stabilization with head movement)
                           - Sensory Reweighting Training (e.g., mCTSIB progression)
                           - Balance Retraining (static → dynamic → functional)
                           - Gait Training with Head Movements and Dual-Task

                           > 🔍 Why? To promote substitution (using vision and somatosensation) and adaptation.

                           Gaze Stabilization Exercise (VOR Substitution):
                           1. Sit → patient fixates on a target
                           2. Therapist moves patient’s head left/right at 1–2 Hz
                           3. Patient must keep eyes on target
                           4. Progress to standing, walking, dual-task

                           > ⚠️ Feet on ground during transitions ← SAFETY  
                           > ✅ Hold shoulders when needed to prevent fall

                           ---

                           ## 6º. HOW WOULD YOU ASSESS DIFFICULTY?

                           Use objective and subjective measures:

                           - Symptoms: Rate dizziness/nausea 0–10 before/during/after
                           - Vital Signs: BP, HR (especially if orthostatic)
                           - RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion): 0–10
                           - Functional Tests: Repeat FGA or BBS to track progress
                           - DHI (Dizziness Handicap Inventory): Patient-reported disability

                           > 🔁 You were marked down for not measuring symptoms to progress/regress treatment.

                           ---

                           ## 7º. HOW WOULD YOU PROGRESS/REGRESS THE TREATMENT?

                           ### 🔁 Progression:
                           - Increase head movement speed
                           - Add dual-task (walk and talk)
                           - Reduce base of support (tandem stance)
                           - Add unstable surfaces (foam)
                           - Increase complexity of gait (obstacles, stairs)

                           ### 🔁 Regression:
                           - Slow down head movements
                           - Use visual cues
                           - Reduce duration
                           - Perform seated first
                           - Provide hand support

                           > 📊 Use symptom response to guide:  
                           > - < 3/10 → progress  
                           > - > 5/10 → regress or stop

                              - Use a cane in low light

                           4. Red Flags:

                           ## 🧪 PATIENT CASE 15  
                           ### Γ(Cerebellar Stroke (Infarct))

                           This is a high-stakes, high-yield case — cerebellar infarction is a central vestibular disorder that can mimic peripheral vertigo (like vestibular neuritis or BPPV), but it is medically emergent and requires immediate referral if not already diagnosed.

                           Unlike peripheral vestibular disorders, which affect the inner ear, cerebellar stroke involves the central nervous system — specifically, the cerebellum, which is critical for coordination, balance, and vestibular integration.

                           This case will challenge your ability to:
                           - Differentiate central from peripheral vertigo using bedside oculomotor exams (HINTS)
                           - Recognize red flags like dysmetria, nystagmus direction, and truncal ataxia
                           - Rule out peripheral causes (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
                           - Initiate urgent referral if the diagnosis is not yet confirmed
                           - Provide safe, appropriate rehab once medically cleared

                           We’ll follow your exact learning framework:
                           - Start with Medical Diagnosis (MDx) and Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx) — stated upfront
                           - Provide big picture context
                           - Walk through interview, exam, tests, treatment, progression, education
                           - Emphasize why we do (or don’t do) each step
                           - Compare with other conditions (e.g., vestibular neuritis, BPPV, multiple sclerosis)
                           - Address your past exam feedback (e.g., safety, PLF, motor exam, explanation)

                           Let’s begin.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ Medical Diagnosis (MDx):  
                           Right Cerebellar Infarct (Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery – PICA territory)

                           ### ✅ Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx):  
                           1. Impaired dynamic balance and coordination associated with cerebellar dysfunction  
                           2. Impaired functional mobility associated with truncal ataxia and gait instability  
                           3. Impaired motor control of movement associated with dysmetria and intention tremor

                           > 🔍 Why these PT diagnoses?  
                           > - #1 is the primary PT diagnosis — the cerebellum is essential for balance control and coordination.  
                           > - #2 reflects that the patient has gait instability, especially on uneven surfaces or with dual-task.  
                           > - #3 captures dysmetria (overshooting) and intention tremor, which are hallmark signs of cerebellar lesions.

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In vestibular neuritis, PT Dx is impaired postural control due to unilateral vestibular hypofunction — peripheral, not central.  
                           > - In BPPV, PT Dx is impaired balance due to positional vertigo — episodic, not constant.  
                           > - In cerebellar stroke, the impairment is central, constant, and progressive — red flag for referral.

                           > 📌 Key Point: The PT diagnosis reflects the movement system impairment, not the medical diagnosis. But the treatment approach changes dramatically based on the underlying pathology.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: Where Does This Case Fit?

                           All vertigo and imbalance cases fall into two main categories:

                           ### 🌐 1. Vestibular System Disorders
                              - Peripheral (inner ear): BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis
                              - Central (brain): Stroke, MS, tumor, vestibular migraine

                           This is central, specifically cerebellar infarction — a life-threatening condition that often presents with:
                           - Sudden onset vertigo
                           - Nausea, vomiting
                           - Gait ataxia
                           - Truncal instability
                           - Dysmetria
                           - Abnormal eye movements

                           #### 🔹 Key Features of Cerebellar Stroke:
                           - Sudden onset of vertigo (often mistaken for BPPV or vestibular neuritis)
                           - No hearing loss (vs. AICA stroke)
                           - Truncal ataxia (can’t sit without support)
                           - Dysmetria (Finger-to-Nose, Heel-to-Shin)
                           - Intention tremor
                           - Nystagmus: downbeat, torsional, or gaze-evoked
                           - Normal Head Impulse Test (HIT) (vs. peripheral vestibulopathy)

                           > ✅ Why this matters:  
                           > - If you treat it like BPPV, you’ll perform an Epley maneuver — which won’t help and may worsen symptoms.  
                           > - If you miss central signs, you might delay life-saving intervention.  
                           > - If you see downbeat nystagmus, suspect central lesion (e.g., PICA or AICA stroke).

                           Our job is to:
                           1. Confirm it’s cerebellar stroke (if not already diagnosed)
                           2. Rule out peripheral causes (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
                           3. Initiate urgent referral if not already evaluated
                           4. Provide safe, compensatory rehab once medically cleared

                           > 🔍 Why these PT diagnoses?

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: Where Does This Case Fit?

                           All vertigo and imbalance cases fall into two main categories:

                           ### 🌐 1. Vestibular System Disorders
                              - Peripheral (inner ear): BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis
                              - Central (brain): Stroke, MS, tumor, vestibular migraine

                           This is central, specifically cerebellar hemorrhage — a life-threatening condition that often presents with:
                           - Sudden onset vertigo
                           - Severe nausea and vomiting
                           - Headache
                           - Truncal ataxia
                           - Dysmetria
                           - Abnormal eye movements

                           #### 🔹 Key Features of Cerebellar Hemorrhage:
                           - Sudden onset of vertigo (often mistaken for BPPV or vestibular neuritis)
                           - Severe headache, often occipital
                           - Projectile vomiting
                           - Altered mental status (drowsiness, confusion)
                           - Truncal ataxia (can’t sit without support)
                           - Dysmetria (Finger-to-Nose, Heel-to-Shin)
                           - Nystagmus: downbeat, torsional, or gaze-evoked
                           - Normal Head Impulse Test (HIT) (vs. peripheral vestibulopathy)

                           > ✅ Why this matters:  
                           > - If you treat it like BPPV, you’ll perform an Epley maneuver — which won’t help and may worsen symptoms.  
                           > - If you miss central signs, you might delay life-saving intervention.  
                           > - If you see downbeat nystagmus, suspect central lesion (e.g., PICA or AICA stroke).

                           Our job is to:
                           1. Confirm it’s cerebellar hemorrhage (if not already diagnosed)
                           2. Rule out peripheral causes (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
                           3. Initiate urgent referral if not already evaluated
                           4. Provide safe, compensatory rehab once medically cleared

                           ## 1º. WHAT WOULD YOU ASK IN THE INTERVIEW?

                           Let’s start with the History, which is Step 2.a: History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS).

                           But first — why are we asking this?

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Role of History in Cerebellar Hemorrhage

                           The history is not just about symptoms — it’s about forming hypotheses and ruling out red flags.

                           We use it to:
                           - Localize the system involved (peripheral vs. central)
                           - Rule out dangerous conditions (e.g., stroke, tumor)
                           - Establish baseline function and safety risks
                           - Guide which systems to test next

                           And per your feedback, you missed social history, fall history, and PLF — so we’ll explicitly include and explain them.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ STRUCTURED INTERVIEW QUESTIONS

                           #### A. History of Present Illness (HPI)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Onset: “When did this start?” | Acute vs. chronic process | Sudden onset → stroke or hemorrhage | Gradual onset → degenerative or medication |
                           | Quality: “Is it spinning, lightheaded, or unsteady?” | True vertigo vs. presyncope | Spinning → vestibular. Lightheaded → cardiovascular | Mislabeling dizziness leads to wrong testing pathway |
                           | Duration: “Is it constant or does it come and go?” | Constant → stroke. Episodic → BPPV | Duration helps differentiate |
                           | Triggers: “Does anything make it worse?” | Movement sensitivity | Worse with head motion → stroke. Positional → BPPV | If you don’t ask, you might miss the key diagnostic clue |
                           | Associated Symptoms: “Any double vision, slurred speech, weakness, or numbness?” | CNS involvement | Double vision → brainstem. Weakness → stroke | Missing neurologic symptoms could delay life-saving referral |
                           | Course: “Is it getting better, worse, or coming and going?” | Progression pattern | Worsening → hemorrhage. Improving → peripheral lesion |
                           | Medications: “Are you on blood pressure meds?” | HTN control | Poorly controlled HTN → risk for hemorrhage | You must monitor BP closely

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In vestibular neuritis, vertigo is constant, movement-sensitive, but no headache or vomiting  
                           > - In cerebellar hemorrhage, it’s constant, with severe headache and projectile vomiting

                           ---

                           #### B. Past Medical History (PMH)

                           Ask:
                           - “Any history of stroke, diabetes, Parkinson’s, ear infections?”  
                           - “Neck problems or head injuries?”  
                           - Why? These can mimic or contribute to dizziness.

                           > In this case: Hypertension → major risk factor for hemorrhagic stroke.

                           ---

                           #### C. Medications & Allergies

                           - “What medications are you taking?”  
                           - Why? Antihypertensives → monitor for orthostasis. No anticoagulants → lower bleeding risk.

                           > In this case: Labetalol IV → BP control critical.

                           ---

                           #### D. Social History, Fall History, and Prior Level of Function (PLF) ← YOU MISSED THIS LAST TIME

                           | Question | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Do you live alone or with someone?” | Safety, home environment, support system | Living alone → high fall risk | Without this, you can’t assess safety or design safe HEP |
                           | “Before this started, could you walk independently? Do you drive?” | PLF = baseline for goals | Was he independent? Driving? Climbing stairs? | You can’t measure progress without knowing baseline |
                           | “Have you fallen? How many times? Any injuries?” | Red flag for injury risk | “Have you fallen?” → yes, once | Falls = high risk; affects intervention choices and safety |
                           | “What do you enjoy doing?” | Patient-centered goals | “I walk daily” → functional goal | Guides treatment planning |

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - If he lived alone, we’d emphasize home safety modifications  
                           > - If he had double vision or slurred speech, we’d suspect brainstem compression and refer immediately

                           So we ask these not just for formality — they directly affect treatment decisions and safety.

                           - “What would you like to be able to do again?”

                           ## 2º. WHAT WOULD YOU PRIORITIZE IN THE NEUROLOGIC EXAM?

                           Now, based on the history, we prioritize components of the neurologic exam.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Neurologic Exam Framework

                           The exam follows a hierarchical order:

                           1. Mental Status → Is the patient alert and able to participate?
                           2. Cranial Nerves → Especially II, III, IV, VI, VIII for oculomotor and vestibular function
                           3. Sensory → Is proprioception intact? (dorsal column)
                           4. Motor → Strength, tone, coordination
                           5. Balance & Coordination → Static, dynamic, walking
                           6. Functional Skills → Sit-to-stand, gait, transfers

                           > ⚠️ Why this order? Because higher-level systems affect lower-level ones. If a patient is confused or has gaze palsy, balance testing may be invalid.

                           ---

                           - Mini-BESTest – Specifically assesses balance control systems

                           ## 🧪 PATIENT CASE 17  
                           ### Γ(Brainstem Stroke)

                           This is a high-stakes, complex case — brainstem stroke is one of the most dangerous central vestibular disorders because it affects vital life-sustaining functions (e.g., breathing, heart rate, consciousness) and critical sensorimotor pathways.

                           Unlike cerebellar stroke, which primarily affects balance and coordination, brainstem stroke can disrupt:
                           - Cranial nerve function (III–XII)
                           - Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)
                           - Sensory and motor tracts (spinothalamic, corticospinal)
                           - Autonomic regulation
                           - Level of consciousness

                           This case will challenge your ability to:
                           - Differentiate brainstem from cerebellar and peripheral causes of vertigo
                           - Perform and interpret cranial nerve exams, HINTS exam, and oculomotor testing
                           - Recognize red flags like dysphagia, dysarthria, Horner’s syndrome, and crossed sensory/motor deficits
                           - Understand that PT intervention is contraindicated in the acute phase unless medically cleared
                           - Provide safe, compensatory rehab once stable

                           We’ll follow your exact learning framework:
                           - Start with Medical Diagnosis (MDx) and Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx) — stated upfront
                           - Provide big picture context

                           ## 1º. WHAT WOULD YOU ASK IN THE INTERVIEW?

                           Let’s start with the History, which is Step 2.a: History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS).

                           But first — why are we asking this?

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Role of History in Brainstem Stroke

                           The history is not just about symptoms — it’s about forming hypotheses and ruling out red flags.

                           We use it to:
                           - Localize the system involved (peripheral vs. central)
                           - Rule out dangerous conditions (e.g., stroke, tumor)
                           - Establish baseline function and safety risks
                           - Guide which systems to test next

                           And per your feedback, you missed social history, fall history, and PLF — so we’ll explicitly include and explain them.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ STRUCTURED INTERVIEW QUESTIONS

                           #### A. History of Present Illness (HPI)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Onset: “When did this start?” | Acute vs. chronic process | Sudden onset → stroke or neuritis | Gradual onset → degenerative or medication |
                           | Quality: “Is it spinning, lightheaded, or unsteady?” | True vertigo vs. presyncope | Spinning → vestibular. Lightheaded → cardiovascular | Mislabeling dizziness leads to wrong testing pathway |
                           | Duration: “Is it constant or does it come and go?” | Constant → stroke. Episodic → BPPV | Duration helps differentiate |
                           | Triggers: “Does anything make it worse?” | Movement sensitivity | Worse with head motion → stroke. Positional → BPPV | If you don’t ask, you might miss the key diagnostic clue |
                           | Associated Symptoms: “Any double vision, slurred speech, weakness, or numbness?” | CNS involvement | Double vision → brainstem. Weakness → stroke | Missing neurologic symptoms could delay life-saving referral |
                           | Swallowing: “Any difficulty swallowing or hoarseness?” | Cranial nerve involvement | Dysphagia → CN IX, X. Hoarseness → CN X | Red flag for aspiration risk |
                           | Facial Sensation: “Any numbness on one side of your face?” | CN V involvement | Ipsilateral facial numbness → brainstem stroke | Key sign of lateral medullary infarct |

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In vestibular neuritis, vertigo is constant, movement-sensitive, but no cranial nerve deficits  
                           > - In brainstem stroke, it’s constant, with dysphagia, dysarthria, and Horner’s

                           ---

                           #### B. Past Medical History (PMH)

                           Ask:
                           - “Any history of stroke, diabetes, Parkinson’s, ear infections?”  
                           - “Neck problems or head injuries?”  
                           - Why? These can mimic or contribute to dizziness.

                           > In this case: Atrial fibrillation → cardioembolic stroke risk.

                           ---

                           #### C. Medications & Allergies

                           - “What medications are you taking?”  
                           - Why? Anticoagulants → fall risk. Vestibular suppressants → delay compensation.

                           > In this case: Apixaban → high fall risk — must use gait belt and supervise closely.

                           |--------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Do you live alone or with someone?” | Safety, home environment, support system | Living with husband → may reduce fall risk | Without this, you can’t assess safety or design safe HEP |
                           | “Before this started, could you walk independently? Do you drive?” | PLF = baseline for goals | Was she independent? Driving? Climbing stairs? | You can’t measure progress without knowing baseline |
                           | “Have you fallen? How many times? Any injuries?” | Red flag for injury risk | “Have you fallen?” → no, but fearful | Falls = high risk; affects intervention choices and safety |
                           | “What do you enjoy doing?” | Patient-centered goals | “I walk daily” → functional goal | Guides treatment planning |

                           ### 🧩 CLINICAL REASONING MAP: Where Does This Fit?

                           All these questions are part of Step 2: History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS).

                           This step helps us:
                           - Form hypotheses (e.g., “This sounds like brainstem stroke”)
                           - Decide what systems to test next
                           - Identify red flags (e.g., sudden vertigo + ataxia = possible stroke)
                           - Establish baseline function and safety concerns

                           > 🔁 Reminder: The Review of Systems (ROS) is a screening tool to rule in/out system involvement. If positive, we do a further detailed examination.

                           ## 2º. WHAT WOULD YOU PRIORITIZE IN THE NEUROLOGIC EXAM?

                           Now, based on the history, we prioritize components of the neurologic exam.

                           From the chart:  
                           > “Sudden vertigo, ipsilateral facial numbness, contralateral body numbness, dysphagia, Horner’s, MRI-confirmed lateral medullary infarct”

                           👉 This is classic Right Lateral Medullary Infarct (Wallenberg Syndrome) — a central vestibular disorder.

                           But we must rule out peripheral causes and assess safety.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Neurologic Exam Framework

                           The exam follows a hierarchical order:

                           1. Mental Status → Is the patient alert and able to participate?
                           2. Cranial Nerves → Especially II, III, IV, VI, VIII for oculomotor and vestibular function
                           3. Sensory → Is proprioception intact? (dorsal column)
                           4. Motor → Strength, tone, coordination
                           5. Balance & Coordination → Static, dynamic, walking
                           6. Functional Skills → Sit-to-stand, gait, transfers

                           > ⚠️ Why this order? Because higher-level systems affect lower-level ones. If a patient is confused or has gaze palsy, balance testing may be invalid.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ PRIORITIZED EXAM COMPONENTS FOR THIS PATIENT

                           We’ll go through each, explaining why, what we’re looking for, and how it fits into the bigger picture.

                           ---

                           #### 2.a. History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS)

                           Already done above.

                           Now, during observation:
                           - Watch how she enters the clinic: wide-based, staggering gait? Trunk sway?
                           - Does she speak slowly or hoarsely?
                           - Why? Natural movement reveals brainstem dysfunction.

                           ---

                           #### 2.b. Sensory Exam

                           We focus on systems relevant to balance:

                           1. Light Touch – Screen dermatomes (e.g., L5-S1)  
                              - Why? Rule out peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy.

                           2. Proprioception (Joint Position Sense) – Big toe up/down  
                              - Why? This tests the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway. Impaired proprioception → poor balance, especially in dark.

                           > 🔄 Compare: In brainstem stroke, proprioception is intact — imbalance is due to poor integration, not sensory loss.

                           ---

                           #### 3.c. Balance Exam

                           This is critical for dizziness.

                           Breakdown:
                           - Static Standing Balance: Sensory orientation & reactive control
                           - Dynamic Standing Balance: Self-generated control
                           - Walking Balance

                           Use standardized tools:
                           - Berg Balance Scale (BBS) – Static and dynamic balance
                           - Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) – Walking with head turns, eyes closed
                           - Mini-BESTest – Specifically assesses balance control systems

                           > 🔍 Why these? Because they’re evidence-based, valid, and responsive to change in vestibular patients.

                           ---

                           #### 4.d. Mental Status Exam

                           Quick screen:
                           - Alertness: Is she awake and responsive?
                           - Orientation: Person, place, time
                           - Attention: Can she follow 2-step commands?
                           - Why? To ensure she can participate in rehab. Cognitive impairment changes treatment approach.

                           ---

                           #### 5.e. Motor Exam

                           Key elements:

                           1. Muscle Mass – Any atrophy? (e.g., from inactivity)
                           2. ROM – Cervical rotation? Limited ROM may cause cervicogenic dizziness.
                           3. Tone – Normal? Spasticity suggests UMN lesion.
                           4. Strength – Manual muscle testing (MMT) of legs and neck
                              - Why? Weakness contributes to imbalance.
                           5. Motor Control – Can she isolate head movements?
                           6. Involuntary Movements – Tremor? Nystagmus?

                           > 🔄 Compare: In brainstem stroke, strength is normal, but coordination is impaired.

                           ---

                           #### 6.f. Functional Skills Exam and Movement Analysis

                           Observe:
                           - Sit-to-Stand: Smooth? Uses arms?  
                           - Transfers: Needs help?  
                           - Walking: Wide base? Truncal sway?  
                           - Stairs: Can she do them?

                           Use Movement Analysis Worksheet to note:
                           - Truncal ataxia
                           - Step length asymmetry
                           - Head-trunk dissociation

                           > 🔄 Compare: In brainstem stroke, gait is wide-based, irregular, with truncal sway.

                           ---

                           #### 7.g. Cranial Nerve Integrity Exam

                           Prioritize:
                           - CN II (Optic): Visual acuity, visual fields  
                           - CN III, IV, VI: Extraocular movements (H-test), saccades, smooth pursuit, convergence  
                           - CN V (Trigeminal): Facial sensation (ipsilateral numbness)  
                           - CN VII (Facial): Facial movement  
                           - CN VIII (Vestibulocochlear): Hearing (whisper test), VOR (HIT), nystagmus  
                           - CN IX, X (Glossopharyngeal, Vagus): Gag reflex, voice quality  
                           - CN XI (Accessory): SCM, trapezius  
                           - CN XII (Hypoglossal): Tongue protrusion

                           > 🔍 Why? To assess oculomotor and vestibular function — central to dizziness.

                           ---

                           #### 8.h. Coordination Exam

                           - Finger to nose
                           - Heel to shin
                           - Rapid alternating movement

                           > 🔄 Compare: In brainstem stroke, coordination is impaired. In BPPV, it’s normal.

                           ---

                           ## 3º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT TO RULE OUT BPPV

                           Now, we rule out BPPV using positional testing.

                           ### ✅ TESTS TO RULE OUT BPPV

                           1. Dix-Hallpike Maneuver  
                              - Purpose: Diagnose posterior canal BPPV  
                              - How: Sit → quickly lay back, head 20° below table, turned 45° to one side  
                              - In this case: Negative bilaterally → rules out posterior canal BPPV

                           2. Supine Roll Test  
                              - Purpose: Diagnose horizontal canal BPPV  
                              - How: Lie on back → rapidly roll head 90° left/right  
                              - In this case: Negative bilaterally → rules out horizontal canal BPPV

                           > ⚠️ Safety: Feet on ground or supported during all tests. You were marked down for this.

                           ---

                           ## 4º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT (General)

                           Now, broader vestibular and oculomotor screening:

                           ### ✅ VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening)

                           From your files: VOMS includes:
                           1. Smooth Pursuits – Follow finger slowly side to side  
                              - Abnormal: Saccadic (jumpy) tracking → cerebellar/brainstem
                           2. Saccades – Rapid shift between two targets  
                              - Abnormal: Overshoot/undershoot → frontal lobe, basal ganglia
                           3. Near Point Convergence – Finger moves toward nose  
                              - Abnormal: Double vision before 5–7 cm → midbrain or CN III
                           4. VOR (Head Impulse Test)  
                              - How: Small, quick head turn left/right while patient fixates on your nose  
                              - Positive: Catch-up saccade → ipsilateral vestibular hypofunction
                              - Why? Tests high-frequency VOR — if impaired, patient can’t stabilize gaze during walking
                           5. Positional Testing – Already done (Dix-Hallpike, Supine Roll)

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - BPPV: Positive Dix-Hallpike, normal VOR  
                           > - Brainstem Stroke: Abnormal saccades/pursuits, downbeat nystagmus, normal HIT

                           ## 5º. WHAT TREATMENT WOULD YOU PROVIDE?

                           ### ✅ For Brainstem Stroke: Wait and Monitor

                           - No active PT intervention in acute phase (first 72 hours)
                           - Monitor for signs of deterioration: worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness
                           - Once stable, begin static balance training, coordination drills, gait training

                           > 🔍 Why? Brainstem stroke can cause respiratory failure or hydrocephalus — PT is contraindicated until medically cleared.

                           Balance Training (when cleared):
                           1. Sit-to-stand → progress to tandem stance
                           2. Use gait belt and close supervision due to fall risk

                           > ⚠️ Feet on ground during transitions ← SAFETY  
                           > ✅ Use gait belt — she’s at risk for falls

                           ---

                           ## 6º. HOW WOULD YOU ASSESS DIFFICULTY?

                           Use objective and subjective measures:

                           - Symptoms: Rate dizziness/nausea 0–10 before/during/after
                           - Vital Signs: BP, HR (especially if orthostatic)
                           - RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion): 0–10
                           - Functional Tests: Repeat FGA or BBS to track progress
                           - DHI (Dizziness Handicap Inventory): Patient-reported disability

                           > 🔁 You were marked down for not measuring symptoms to progress/regress treatment.

                           ---

                           ## 7º. HOW WOULD YOU PROGRESS/REGRESS THE TREATMENT?

                           ### 🔁 Progression:
                           - Add dual-task (walk and talk)
                           - Reduce base of support (tandem stance)
                           - Add unstable surfaces (foam)
                           - Increase speed of movements

                           ### 🔁 Regression:
                           - Use visual cues
                           - Reduce duration
                           - Perform seated first
                           - Provide hand support

                           > 📊 Use symptom response to guide:  
                           > - < 3/10 → progress  
                           > - > 5/10 → regress or stop

                           ## 🧪 PATIENT CASE 18  
                           ### Γ(Multiple Sclerosis (MS))

                           This is a complex, relapsing-remitting case — Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can affect any level of the neuraxis, leading to multifocal neurological symptoms.

                           Unlike acute stroke or BPPV, MS is not a single-event disorder. It is characterized by episodic attacks (relapses) followed by periods of partial or complete recovery (remission), and over time, it can lead to progressive disability.

                           This case will challenge your ability to:
                           - Recognize multisystem involvement (vestibular, oculomotor, motor, sensory)
                           - Differentiate central from peripheral vertigo using bedside oculomotor exams (HINTS)
                           - Identify key signs like nystagmus, dysmetria, Uhthoff’s phenomenon, and fatigue
                           - Understand that PT intervention is safe and essential for symptom management and functional maintenance
                           - Provide clear patient education about energy conservation, fall prevention, and temperature sensitivity

                           We’ll follow your exact learning framework:
                           - Start with Medical Diagnosis (MDx) and Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx) — stated upfront
                           - Provide big picture context
                           - Walk through interview, exam, tests, treatment, progression, education
                           - Emphasize why we do (or don’t do) each step
                           - Compare with other conditions (e.g., stroke, BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
                           - Address your past exam feedback (e.g., safety, PLF, motor exam, explanation)

                           Let’s begin.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ Medical Diagnosis (MDx):  
                           Multiple Sclerosis (Relapsing-Remitting Type)  
                           - Active lesion in the brainstem and cerebellar pathways  
                           - Current relapse: vertigo, imbalance, and gait ataxia

                           ### ✅ Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx):  
                           1. Impaired dynamic balance and coordination associated with central vestibular dysfunction  
                           2. Impaired functional mobility associated with gait ataxia and postural instability  
                           3. Impaired motor control of movement associated with dysmetria and oculomotor dysfunction

                           > 🔍 Why these PT diagnoses?  
                           > - #1 is the primary PT diagnosis — MS lesions in the brainstem/cerebellum disrupt vestibular integration, leading to constant imbalance.  
                           > - #2 reflects that the patient has gait instability, especially on uneven surfaces or with dual-task.  
                           > - #3 captures dysmetria (overshooting) and abnormal saccades, which are hallmark signs of CNS demyelination.

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In BPPV, PT Dx is impaired balance due to positional vertigo — episodic, not constant.  
                           > - In vestibular neuritis, PT Dx is impaired postural control due to unilateral vestibular hypofunction — peripheral, not central.  
                           > - In MS, the impairment is central, multifocal, and fluctuating — no Epley maneuver, but VOR and balance training are key.

                           > 📌 Key Point: The PT diagnosis reflects the movement system impairment, not the medical diagnosis. But the treatment approach changes dramatically based on the underlying pathology.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: Where Does This Case Fit?

                           All vertigo and imbalance cases fall into two main categories:

                           ### 🌐 1. Vestibular System Disorders
                              - Peripheral (inner ear): BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis
                              - Central (brain): Stroke, MS, tumor, vestibular migraine

                           This is central, specifically Multiple Sclerosis (MS) — a demyelinating disease that can affect:
                           - Brainstem → vertigo, nystagmus, dysarthria
                           - Cerebellum → ataxia, dysmetria
                           - Spinal cord → weakness, spasticity
                           - Optic nerves → vision loss (optic neuritis)
                           - Cortical pathways → fatigue, cognitive changes

                           #### 🔹 Key Features of MS-Related Vertigo:
                           - Recurrent spontaneous vertigo (not positional)
                           - Nystagmus: horizontal, torsional, or vertical, non-fatiguing
                           - Oculomotor impairments: saccadic pursuit, gaze-evoked nystagmus
                           - Ataxia and gait disturbances
                           - Fatigue (worsens with activity)
                           - Uhthoff’s phenomenon: symptoms worsen with heat or exercise

                           > ✅ Why this matters:  
                           > - If you treat it like BPPV, you’ll perform an Epley maneuver — which won’t help and may worsen symptoms.  
                           > - If you see vertical nystagmus, suspect central lesion (e.g., MS, stroke).  
                           > - If symptoms worsen with heat, think Uhthoff’s phenomenon.

                           Our job is to:
                           1. Confirm it’s MS-related vertigo (not BPPV or stroke)
                           2. Rule out peripheral causes (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
                           3. Initiate vestibular rehab focused on adaptation and substitution
                           4. Educate the patient about fatigue management and fall prevention

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Neurologic Exam Framework

                           The exam follows a hierarchical order:

                           1. Mental Status → Is the patient alert and able to participate?
                           2. Cranial Nerves → Especially II, III, IV, VI, VIII for oculomotor and vestibular function
                           3. Sensory → Is proprioception intact? (dorsal column)
                           4. Motor → Strength, tone, coordination
                           5. Balance & Coordination → Static, dynamic, walking
                           6. Functional Skills → Sit-to-stand, gait, transfers

                           > ⚠️ Why this order? Because higher-level systems affect lower-level ones. If a patient is confused or has gaze palsy, balance testing may be invalid.

                           ### ✅ PRIORITIZED EXAM COMPONENTS FOR THIS PATIENT

                           This is critical for dizziness.

                           - Dynamic Standing Balance: Self-generated control

                           ## 3º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT TO RULE OUT BPPV

                           Now, we rule out BPPV using positional testing.

                           ### ✅ TESTS TO RULE OUT BPPV

                           1. Dix-Hallpike Maneuver  
                              - Purpose: Diagnose posterior canal BPPV  
                              - How: Sit → quickly lay back, head 20° below table, turned 45° to one side  
                              - In this case: Negative bilaterally → rules out posterior canal BPPV

                           2. Supine Roll Test  
                              - Purpose: Diagnose horizontal canal BPPV  
                              - How: Lie on back → rapidly roll head 90° left/right  
                              - In this case: Negative bilaterally → rules out horizontal canal BPPV

                           > ⚠️ Safety: Feet on ground or supported during all tests. You were marked down for this.

                           ---

                           ## 4º. DEMONSTRATE AN ASSESSMENT (General)

                           Now, broader vestibular and oculomotor screening:

                           ### ✅ VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening)

                           From your files: VOMS includes:
                           1. Smooth Pursuits – Follow finger slowly side to side  
                              - Abnormal: Saccadic (jumpy) tracking → cerebellar/brainstem
                           2. Saccades – Rapid shift between two targets  
                              - Abnormal: Overshoot/undershoot → frontal lobe, basal ganglia
                           3. Near Point Convergence – Finger moves toward nose  
                              - Abnormal: Double vision before 5–7 cm → midbrain or CN III
                           4. VOR (Head Impulse Test)  
                              - How: Small, quick head turn left/right while patient fixates on your nose  
                              - Positive: Catch-up saccade → ipsilateral vestibular hypofunction
                              - Why? Tests high-frequency VOR — if impaired, patient can’t stabilize gaze during walking
                           5. Positional Testing – Already done (Dix-Hallpike, Supine Roll)

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - BPPV: Positive Dix-Hallpike, normal VOR  
                           > - MS: Abnormal saccades/pursuits, non-fatiguing nystagmus, normal or abnormal HIT

                           ## 5º. WHAT TREATMENT WOULD YOU PROVIDE?

                           ### ✅ For MS: Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT)

                           - VOR Adaptation Exercises (e.g., VORx1, VORx2)
                           - Balance Retraining (static → dynamic → functional)
                           - Gait Training with Dual-Task
                           - Energy Conservation and Fatigue Management

                           > 🔍 Why? To promote central compensation and functional recovery.

                           VOR Adaptation Exercise (VORx1) for Central Vestibular Dysfunction:
                           1. Sit → patient fixates on a target (e.g., nose)
                           2. Therapist moves patient’s head left/right at 1–2 Hz
                           3. Patient must keep eyes on target
                           4. Progress to standing, walking, dual-task

                           > ⚠️ Feet on ground during transitions ← SAFETY  
                           > ✅ Hold shoulders when needed to prevent fall

                           ---

                           ## 6º. HOW WOULD YOU ASSESS DIFFICULTY?

                           Use objective and subjective measures:

                           - Symptoms: Rate dizziness/nausea 0–10 before/during/after
                           - Vital Signs: BP, HR (especially if orthostatic)
                           - RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion): 0–10
                           - Functional Tests: Repeat FGA or BBS to track progress
                           - DHI (Dizziness Handicap Inventory): Patient-reported disability

                           > 🔁 You were marked down for not measuring symptoms to progress/regress treatment.

                           ---

                           ## 7º. HOW WOULD YOU PROGRESS/REGRESS THE TREATMENT?

                           ### 🔁 Progression:
                           - Increase head movement speed
                           - Add dual-task (walk and talk)
                           - Reduce base of support (tandem stance)
                           - Add unstable surfaces (foam)
                           - Increase complexity of gait (obstacles, stairs)

                           ### 🔁 Regression:
                           - Slow down head movements
                           - Use visual cues
                           - Reduce duration
                           - Perform seated first
                           - Provide hand support

                           > 📊 Use symptom response to guide:  
                           > - < 3/10 → progress  
                           > - > 5/10 → regress or stop

                           ## 🧪 PATIENT CASE 19  
                           ### Γ(Vestibular Migraine)

                           This is a challenging, high-yield case — vestibular migraine is the most common cause of episodic vertigo in adults, affecting 1–2.7% of the general population, and it is frequently misdiagnosed as BPPV, Meniere’s disease, or anxiety.

                           Unlike peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis), vestibular migraine is a central vestibular disorder with no structural lesion, but rather dysfunction in central sensory processing — particularly in how the brain integrates vestibular, visual, and somatosensory input.

                           This case will challenge your ability to:
                           - Differentiate episodic spontaneous vertigo from positional vertigo
                           - Recognize migraine features (photophobia, phonophobia, aura) during vertigo episodes
                           - Rule out peripheral causes (e.g., BPPV, Meniere’s)
                           - Understand that PT intervention is appropriate and evidence-based
                           - Provide clear patient education about triggers, lifestyle modification, and vestibular rehab

                           We’ll follow your exact learning framework:
                           - Start with Medical Diagnosis (MDx) and Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx) — stated upfront
                           - Provide big picture context
                           - Walk through interview, exam, tests, treatment, progression, education
                           - Emphasize why we do (or don’t do) each step
                           - Compare with other conditions (e.g., BPPV, Meniere’s, central stroke)
                           - Address your past exam feedback (e.g., safety, PLF, motor exam, explanation)

                           Let’s begin.

                           ---

                           ### ✅ Medical Diagnosis (MDx):  
                           Vestibular Migraine  
                           - Current episode triggered by stress and lack of sleep
                           - No acute central lesion on MRI (recently cleared by neurology)

                           ### ✅ Physical Therapy Diagnosis(es) (PT Dx):  
                           1. Impaired dynamic balance and coordination associated with episodic central vestibular dysfunction  
                           2. Impaired functional mobility associated with movement-provoked dizziness and visual motion sensitivity  
                           3. Impaired motor control of movement associated with altered sensory integration and heightened symptom response

                           > 🔍 Why these PT diagnoses?  
                           > - #1 is the primary PT diagnosis — the patient has episodic imbalance due to central vestibular processing dysfunction.  
                           > - #2 reflects that the patient is sensitive to visual motion and head movement, which limits function.  
                           > - #3 captures altered sensory integration — common in migraine — where the brain over-relies on vision and under-uses vestibular input.

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In BPPV, PT Dx is impaired balance due to positional vertigo — episodic, positional, fatigable  
                           > - In vestibular neuritis, PT Dx is impaired postural control due to unilateral vestibular hypofunction — constant, not episodic  
                           > - In vestibular migraine, the impairment is episodic, spontaneous, and triggered by sensory overload

                           > 📌 Key Point: The PT diagnosis reflects the movement system impairment, not the medical diagnosis. But the treatment approach changes dramatically based on the underlying pathology.

                           ---

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: Where Does This Case Fit?

                           All vertigo and imbalance cases fall into two main categories:

                           ### 🌐 1. Vestibular System Disorders
                              - Peripheral (inner ear): BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, Meniere’s
                              - Central (brain): Stroke, MS, tumor, vestibular migraine

                           This is central, specifically vestibular migraine — a neurological disorder of sensory processing that affects how the brain handles vestibular, visual, and somatosensory input.

                           #### 🔹 Key Features of Vestibular Migraine:
                           - At least 5 episodes of moderate-to-severe dizziness lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours
                           - History of migraine (with or without aura)
                           - Migraine features in ≥50% of episodes:
                             - Headache (unilateral, pulsating, moderate/severe, worsened by activity)
                             - Photophobia or phonophobia
                             - Visual aura
                           - No better explanation by another vestibular or neurological disorder

                           > ✅ Why this matters:  
                           > - If you treat it like BPPV, you’ll perform an Epley maneuver — which won’t help and may worsen symptoms.  
                           > - If you see positional nystagmus, it may mimic BPPV, but in migraine, it’s persistent and slower than classic BPPV.  
                           > - If you miss photophobia or stress triggers, you might misdiagnose it as anxiety or PPPD.

                           Our job is to:
                           1. Confirm it’s vestibular migraine (not BPPV or Meniere’s)
                           2. Rule out peripheral causes (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
                           3. Initiate vestibular rehab focused on sensory integration and habituation
                           4. Educate the patient about trigger management and lifestyle modification

                           ## 1º. WHAT WOULD YOU ASK IN THE INTERVIEW?

                           Let’s start with the History, which is Step 2.a: History, Observation, and Review of Systems (ROS).

                           But first — why are we asking this?

                           ### 🔍 BIG PICTURE: The Role of History in Vestibular Migraine

                           The history is not just about symptoms — it’s about forming hypotheses and ruling out red flags.

                           We use it to:
                           - Localize the system involved (peripheral vs. central)
                           - Rule out dangerous conditions (e.g., stroke, tumor)
                           - Establish baseline function and safety risks
                           - Guide which systems to test next

                           ---

                           ### ✅ STRUCTURED INTERVIEW QUESTIONS

                           #### A. History of Present Illness (HPI)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Onset: “When did this start?” | Acute vs. chronic process | Episodic → migraine. Sudden → stroke | Helps differentiate vestibular migraine from other conditions |
                           | Quality: “Is it spinning, lightheaded, or unsteady?” | True vertigo vs. presyncope | Spinning → vestibular. Lightheaded → cardiovascular | Mislabeling dizziness leads to wrong testing pathway |
                           | Duration: “How long does it last?” | Minutes to hours → migraine. Seconds → BPPV | Duration helps differentiate |
                           | Triggers: “Does anything make it worse?” | Stress, light, motion, sleep | Worse with light/motion → migraine. Positional → BPPV | If you don’t ask, you might miss the key diagnostic clue |
                           | Associated Symptoms: “Any headache, light/sound sensitivity, or aura?” | Migraine features | Photophobia → migraine. Weakness → stroke | Missing migraine features delays correct diagnosis |
                           | Course: “Is it getting better, worse, or coming and going?” | Episodic → migraine. Constant → neuritis | Helps determine prognosis and urgency |
                           | Medications: “Are you on migraine prophylaxis?” | Medical management | Propranolol, topiramate → may help | You may advise trigger avoidance

                           > 🔄 Compare:  
                           > - In BPPV, vertigo is episodic, <30 sec, positional  
                           > - In vestibular migraine, it’s episodic, 5 min–72 hr, spontaneous or triggered by sensory overload
